body_clean: Chennai: The 18th-century Geology and Anthropology buildings at the Government Museum in Egmore are undergoing a â110 crore conservation makeover by public works department, to be completed by March next year. The conservation work involves roof restoration, flooring, wall plastering, and making the buildings waterproof, PWD officials said. Roof restoration forms a key component of the work. The Geology building has a reddish-brown Mangalore tile roof, a portion of which had collapsed. Roofing in the Anthropology building includes both the sloped Mangalore tile and flat Madras terrace roofing. âThe Anthropology building is a bigger one compared to the Geology building, where work is happening. It is very structurally sound. The bricks and plastering of the old times are still good, and there are unique designs inside,â said a PWD official. The Anthropology building, which has a ground floor and a floor above, has a high ceiling, a stone staircase and a glass ceiling in the middle that allows light into the building. It has Minton tiles dating back to the 1890s, the official said. The Geology building is also undergoing flooring work as per the heritage method, following the same patterns as the original. âWhen it rains, water leaks onto the floor. Work has been carried out to make it waterproof. Doors and windows will also be restored,â the official said. Wall strengthening and crack stitching works are also under way at both buildings, and around 30% of the work is already complete. PWD officials said the project is being undertaken, with the old design and character of the buildings being retained rather than replacing them with modern structures. The 16.25-acre govt museum complex has 48 galleries across six buildings, bringing together collections built over more than a century. The museum began in 1851 with geological collections, following earlier efforts by the Madras Literary Society to establish a Museum of Economic Geology. The collections were then shifted to the Pantheon in 1854. The Anthropology collections also reflect the museumâs long evolution. Ethnology was introduced as a museum subject in 1878, with prehistoric antiquities and ethnographic material becoming part of the collection.

There will be another special TET in Dec this year. The notification for the exam will be released along with the results,â the official said. summary_clean: Inclusive walks with sign language interpreters allow the deaf to experience nature through photography
body_clean: âTt is so quiet out here,â was what one of the hearing impaired participants observed, on taking a walk through Nanmangalam forest. It was 7am and there was just the chirping of birds and insects to be heard. âFor people with hearing impairment who use hearing aids, the urban soundscape can sometimes become overwhelmingly loud,â says Anjana Venkatecan of Care Earth Trust, which collaborated with the Deaf Artists Collective (DFC) to conduct the nature walk recently, along with the Tamil Nadu forest department. âBeing able to access a peaceful place and experience the sounds of nature was a big deal for them,â she says. DFC, a creative community initiative under Madras Photo Bloggers, aims to bridge the accessibility gap by creating meaningful and dignified opportunities for deaf people to explore various spaces. Though they have had photo walks before, this is the first exclusive nature walk for the deaf to be conducted with their communication needs in mind. âWhen it is primarily a photo walk, participants may be more interested in photography than in learning about the environment,â says Anjana. âHaving sign language interpretation and a deaf-friendly environment made it easier for them to participate, learn, connect with others and enjoy the experience without worrying about communication barriers.â Srivatsan Sankaran, founder of Madras Photo Bloggers, says many deaf people do not always get opportunities to experience and capture nature because of communication and accessibility barriers. âMost outdoor activities and nature experiences are designed around hearing-based communication. Information may be given verbally, instructions may be announced without visual alternatives, and sign language interpretation may not be available. We wanted participants to explore and experience nature through photography.â Nanmangalam is a forested area and so spotting birds was difficult, says Anjana. âThat gave us an opportunity to talk more about its flora. The walk was more geared towards insects. We saw a lot of butterflies, stick insects, weaver ants and other insects.â The sign-language interpreter is crucial to the experience. âFrom our side, we had to slightly change our approach to accommodate the interpretation, slow down and factor in the additional time required for signing,â says Anjana. DFC will continue creating more of such inclusive nature walks and photography experiences for the deaf community in different environments, says Srivatsan.

body_clean: Chennai: Anna University and Boeing India Private Limited signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to establish a flammability learning laboratory at the Madras Institute of Technology (MIT) on Tuesday. This will be the first dedicated academic laboratory for flammability research, testing and training. It will serve as an advanced research, testing and training centre in flammability science and safety. âThe facility will provide students with opportunities to develop advanced knowledge and hands-on skills in aerospace flammability,â Anna University registrar (in charge) V Kumaresan said. Boeing will provide equipment to this lab for research and academic purposes. âFlammability testing is an essential aspect of aerospace and product safety, evaluating how easily materials or finished products ignite, burn or continue to burn when exposed to fire or heat,â said Professor C Senthilkumar, head, department of aerospace engineering, MIT. Experts from Boeing will also take classes for MIT students. âWe have engineers from Boeing teaching some courses to our students. This partnership will further boost our cooperation,â Senthilkumar said. Professors said this marks an important step towards developing industry-ready talent and advancing academic capabilities in aerospace safety. MIT was the first institution in the country to launch an aerospace engineering course in 1949. Amirtha Ganesan, manager at Boeing India Private Limited, C Senthilkumar, head, department of aerospace engineering, MIT, and V Kumaresan participated in the event.

title: Checkpoints vanish, helmet violations thrive

body_clean: Chennai: Helmet enforcement for both riders and pillion riders appears to have slackened across the city, with routine checkpoints disappearing from several arterial and interior roads, even as motorists increasingly ride without protective headgear, sometimes carrying three or more people on a two-wheeler. The decline in visible enforcement is noticeable in Saidapet, Guindy, Anna Salai, Royapettah, Porur and several parts of north Chennai, where traffic police personnel were earlier deployed to check violations. Barring a few checkpoints at places such as Moolakothalam junction, Nelson Manickam Road and Anna Nagar, dedicated helmet checks have become less frequent. Barricades remain at some junctions, but the enforcement that once accompanied them appears to have softened. The consequences are visible on the roads. âPeople are riding without helmets and throwing caution to the wind. Earlier, the possibility of being stopped at the next junction acted as a deterrent,â said Vishnu, a resident of Vysarpadi. The easing of enforcement comes at a time when fatalities linked to riding without helmets have increased. In Chennai, 25 people riding without helmets were killed in two-wheeler crashes in the first six months of 2026, compared with 21 during the same period last year. The trend is more pronounced across Tamil Nadu . Of the 4,180 people killed in two-wheeler crashes between Jan and June this year, 1,136 deaths were linked to riders without helmets, compared with 803 during the same period in 2025, an increase of more than 41%. Traffic police personnel say senior officers have instructed personnel to book at least 50 helmet violation cases a day. âInstead of stopping motorists and getting into arguments, personnel have been asked to photograph vehicles and register cases electronically,â said a senior traffic official. Road safety expert P Kamalanathan said sustained enforcement is crucial as even a brief relaxation in checks can encourage motorists to disregard helmet rules.

title: Chennai court grants bail to prime accused in school recognition cheating case

body_clean: CHENNAI: A Chennai special court for corruption cases on Tuesday granted bail to B T Arasakumar, the prime accused in Rs 100cr private school recognition cheating case. The bail is granted âas the indefeasible right to release on bail accrues in favour of the accused following non-filing of final report by the police within the legal time limit,â the court said. "The accused earns this bail not because of merit to his case but due to the default on the part of the investigating agency to complete the investigation within the period stipulated 90 days under BNSS," special judge L S Sathiyamurthy said. Explaining the concept of a default bail, the court said there was no such provision in the old CrPC. It was first introduced in Section167 of CrPC with effect from April 1, 1974. This concept of default bail has been well recognised by the law and courts in India. It has been incorporated in Section 187 (3) in the newly adopted BNSS. This provision, which was adopted without any substantial change or modification from the previous code, is applicable to the present petition on hand. The petitioner has been in incarceration since June 27, and 92 days have lapsed. The Central Crime Branch (CCB), Chennai, has not filed the final report on completion of the investigation, the court said. Further, when this bail application came up for hearing, the police filed a request in writing for extension of time as it has proposed to conduct further searches to collect evidence. Therefore, the investigation is not completed within the stipulated time of 90 days, is a fact not in dispute, the court added. The court was informed that on Sept 28, the Madras high court quashed the detention of the accused under the Goondas Act.

title: Chennai district urges public to report unlicensed child care homes

body_clean: Chennai: Chennai district administration has urged the public to report child care homes operating without govt authorisation and any form of abuse or mistreatment of children. There are 91 children's homes in Chennai city; however, many function without proper recognition or a licence. Chennai district collector S Malathi Helen said complaints and information about unauthorised child care homes and incidents of abuse could be reported to District Child Protection Unit (DCPU). DCPU functions under the Department of Child Welfare and Special Services, the Union Ministry of Women and Child Development, and the state social welfare and nutritious meal programme dept. The unit undertakes several activities, including registration and inspection of child care homes, conducting meetings of child care home management committees, providing financial assistance, identifying foster care parents, creating awareness among the public about child protection and providing capacity-building training to government and private sector officials. It also conducts district-level advisory committee meetings and prepares information, education and awareness materials. There are several child care homes run by voluntary organisations in Chennai. The administration said these homes are required to be registered and operate in accordance with the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, including the amended provisions of 2006 and 2015. People can submit complaints regarding child care homes functioning without govt authorisation, as well as any form of abuse or mistreatment of children, to the District Child Protection Unit. Complaints can be submitted to the District Child Protection Officer, District Child Protection Unit, No. 300, Purasawalkam High Road, Kellys, Chennai-10. The unit can be contacted at 044-25952450 or 6369124017. Complaints can also be emailed to dcpschennai2022@gmail.com.

title: Chennai Metro phase-2 stretch to open on Oct 11; trains will not be driverless until mid-2027
title_clean: Chennai Metro phase-2 stretch to open on Oct 11; trains will not be driverless until mid-2027
title_normalized: chennai metro phase 2 stretch to open on oct 11 trains will not be driverless until mid 2027
body_clean: Chennai: The first stretch of Chennai Metroâs Phase-2 network, from Poonamallee Bypass to Vadapalani, covering 14.64km, will be inaugurated on Oct 11, but trains will not run in driverless mode until mid-2027. CMRL officials said Prime Minister Narendra Modi will inaugurate the line and is expected to take a ride on one of the trains. The 14.64km stretch has 17 stations in all, but only 11 will initially open to passengers, with trains bypassing six stations â Alapakkam, Karambakkam, Valasaravakkam, Alwarthirunagar, Saligramam and Avichi School â on the double-decker section between Porur Junction and Vadapalani. The inauguration comes nearly seven months after CMRL received conditional approval from the CMRS in Feb and subsequently secured final authorisation, with relaxations in train speed and frequency, in May. The trains are designed for Unattended Train Operation (UTO) without operators assistance, but will initially run in Automatic Train Operation (ATO) mode, with two train operators onboard supervising the service. Under ATO, acceleration, braking, stopping and speed regulation are automated, but staff remain onboard to monitor operations and intervene when required. UTO allows these functions, including door control and routine train movements, to be handled automatically under the supervision of the Operation Control Centre (OCC) located in Koyambedu and a backup OCC in Nandanam. âWe will have two operators onboard all the trains and operate them in degraded mode. It means the operator will have to apply brakes manually as the signalling system and trains are not synced. We will go driverless by mid-2027,â an official said. The second operator will monitor signals and assist during emergencies. The official said UTO testing was under way, with 120 test cases or scenarios to be validated before CMRL applies for CMRS certification. Testing will continue between midnight and 5am after passenger services begin. Fifteen trains will initially operate at 10-minute intervals. The maximum fare between Vadapalani and Poonamallee Bypass will be â140, while a journey from Poonamallee Bypass to Airport, Egmore or Central railway station will cost â150. The trains have a maximum design speed of 80kmph but will average 32kmph, slowing to 25-30kmph on two curves. Each three-car train can carry up to 900 passengers. In comparison, Phase-1 trains operate with integrated signalling that automatically triggers braking or speed reduction based on signals. The four-car trains have a capacity of 1,270 passengers and an average operating speed of 34kmph. At present, Delhi Metro operates UTO services in India. Metro systems in Singapore, Dubai and several European cities also operate driverless services.

body_clean: Chennai: It was an unusual Sunday on First Avenue in Indira Nagar, Adyar, which is largely deserted during weekends. Customers thronged the road, which houses seven branches of public- and private-sector banks, including a small finance bank, within a 400m radius. The footfall was higher at public-sector banks in anticipation of banking operations being disrupted in view of the three-day strike called by bank unions between Sept 28 and 30, which has been deferred after meeting between banksâ association and unions. Banks were open on Sunday to offset the impact of the strike, as operations in public-sector banks and some old-generation private-sector banks were likely to be affected between Monday and Wednesday. However, branches of new-generation private-sector lenders were to remain open. There was a stark difference in footfall, with several bank branches in north Chennai being more crowded compared with those in the southern and central parts of the city. Senior citizens outnumbered other customers, while several visited for cash deposits and withdrawals, cheque clearances, and account-related queries. S Sundararajan, 77, who visited a Bank of India branch in Adyar for an account-related query, recalled how banks used to operate on Sundays for the convenience of residents. âI am a former bank employee and was part of the Sunday operations, though it was several years ago. Such branches used to function additionally on Sundays, mostly in residential locations,â he said. In north Chennai, the branches were thronged by a sizeable number of senior citizens to withdraw their pensions. Mohamed Asik, a visitor to an SBI branch in Washermenpet, said another reason for this was the convenience of Sunday operations. âMany have free time only on Sundays, and they used this opportunity to visit their respective branches,â he added. Banks were prepared for higher transaction volumes on Sunday. Indian Bank anticipated Sundayâs transaction volumes could be higher and prepared for this in advance. âOur branches and offices have been provided with adequate manpower, and our ATMs were replenished beforehand to ensure sufficient cash availability. As our currency chests are operational, the cash requirements of linked branches and ATMs are being taken care of,â a senior Indian Bank official said.

body_clean: Chennai: Not just people with poor digital literacy fall prey to cyber fraud . Highly educated individuals with experience in using digital services can also fall victim to such crimes, a new study led by IIT Madras has found. The study examined 33 financial cybercrime victims in five cities â Chennai, Bengaluru, Mumbai, New Delhi and Hyderabad. The victims included IT professionals, investment bankers, doctors, public-sector officials and others with expertise in information technology, finance and cybersecurity. They were targeted through scams, including fake digital arrest threats, investment fraud, task-based fraud, and payment scams. Their financial losses ranged from a few thousand rupees to more than â11 crore. Several victims reported shame, insomnia, depression, and strained relationships with family members. âOur findings show that even highly educated people who use smartphones, online banking, UPI , and other digital services can become vulnerable,â said professor Nandan Sudarsanam of the Wadhwani School of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence at IIT Madras. Professor P Kandaswamy, a retired IPS officer and adjunct faculty member at the department of data science and AI at IIT Madras, said fraudsters often exploited victims during periods of personal stress and disruption. âVictims were approached when they were dealing with illness, family responsibilities, retirement, job-related pressure or financial uncertainty. Scamsters then used fear, urgency, coercion and promises of financial gain to influence their decisions,â he said. Researchers conducted semi-structured interviews with victims from varied age groups, genders and socio-economic backgrounds. The study was recently published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. The research team also included Akanksha Jaiswal, from the University of Western Australia, Chennai campus, and Ameeta Fernando of the Loyola Institute of Business Administration. âThe response to cybercrime must move beyond blaming victims. Banks and law-enforcement agencies need stronger systems for early detection, rapid intervention, and coordinated response, along with better support for victims,â Kandhaswamy said. The researchers recommended moving beyond generic âbe careful onlineâ messaging and adopting targeted awareness campaigns based on specific fraud tactics and vulnerable situations.

The FIR said 45.72 lakh cubic feet of sand was removed from Malappambadi Lake and transported to level a 124-acre property belonging to Kumaran for the DMKâs northern regional conference held in Dec 2025. The DVAC said its verification revealed that Arunai Products and Services Ltd, in which Kumaran is a director, purchased 124.56 acres from Rishi Enterprises for â146 crore. Rishi Enterprises is owned by P Jeyalakshmi, wife of highways contractor Pandithurai, the DVAC said. Citing district gazette notifications, the sleuths said Malappambadi Lake was not among the waterbodies identified for removal of silt or gravel for agricultural purposes. It said Kumaran submitted two applications seeking permission to remove clay/silt from Palliyampattu Lake on Oct 31 and Nov 27, 2025. Officials from the revenue, geology and mining departments, besides the corporation, failed to discharge their statutory duties, thereby facilitating the illegal removal of sand, the DVAC said. âSuch deliberate and wilful inaction, despite knowledge of the illegal excavation, prima facie, indicates connivance with persons involved,â the DVAC said. The sleuths said the influence of Velu and his son in the matter cannot be ruled out and requires investigation, along with the role of others involved.

body_clean: Chennai: Temple is an âestablishmentâ and hence the families of its employees who die while on duty are entitled to compensation as workmen, ruled Madras high court , confirming a decision of the joint commissioner of labour. Arulmigu Theertha Paleswarar Thirukoil in Triplicane engaged a private security firm to secure its premises. After he died while on duty, his family approached the labour department for compensation. After the joint commissioner of labour upheld their request, the temple administration moved the high court against it. Justice K Surender passed the order while dismissing an appeal by the temple management against the order passed by the labour commissioner dated July 28, 2022. âThe fact that the deceased was engaged and paid by a private security firm may be relevant for determining the ultimate liability and the quantum of compensation. However, the same would not, at this stage, render the claim proceedings non-maintainable. In such circumstances, this court finds no ground to interfere with the order passed by the labour commissioner,â the court said. Since the claim proceedings relate to 2021, the labour commissioner shall expedite the proceedings and conclude the determination of the claim on merits and in accordance with law, preferably within six weeks, the court added. According to B Sridevi, wife of the deceased security guard, her husband Babu, was working as a security guard in the premises of the temple. On July 17, 2021, when he was guarding the temple premises during the night, certain miscreants entered the temple premises with an intention to commit theft. When Babu attempted to prevent the theft, he was attacked by the persons, sustained grievous injuries to his head, and succumbed to the injuries, she said.

On Wednesday morning, residents spotted the body near the shore and alerted police. The body was sent to Kilpauk govt hospital for postmortem. Police investigation found that there had been a financial dispute between the deceased and Sanjay and Hari. GCC commissioner G S Sameeran inspected the trial around 10am near Madras Medical College (MMC) studentsâ hostel. The trial was held where the North Buckingham Canal meets the Cooum. Sameeran said this would counter Culexmosquitoes, a common genus of medium-sized mosquitoes, and their larvae. The civic body will use drones on waterways wider than 30m in every zone. The city recorded nearly 8,300 fever cases by the end of Sept. Of these, 1,775 tested positive for dengue. âFever trends in the city have been high over the past two months,â Sameeran told reporters. But more than 90% of the cases are self-limiting, he said. GCC identified 539 mosquito-breeding hotspots where larval levels exceed the corporationâs threshold and is carrying out focused vector-control measures in these areas. The Breteau Index, which measures live mosquito larvae in 100 inspected houses, is now 0.46 in Chennai. While the index should not exceed 5, GCC designates areas with a reading above 0.1 as hotspots. GCC has also collected â17.2 lakh in fines for repeated violations such as dumping garbage or leaving water containers uncovered. Sameeran urged residents to remove small containers, cups, plates, broken items and old tyres from their surroundings.

An existing 350m lined drain inside IIT Madras will be connected to a double-vent, cut-and-cover stormwater drain leading to south Buckingham Canal. The project has been divided into two packages, said GCC commissioner G S Sameeran. âIn the first package, 40m of work remains. Top slab concreting work is underway, and will be completed in 10 days,â he said. The second package will take another 20 days. âItâs highly complex because we have to cross Old Mahabalipuram Road, which is also the entry point for Chennai Metro Rail Limitedâs underground station tunnel boring machine,â Sameeran said. A 90m stretch is yet to be built to connect the drain to south Buckingham Canal. The commissioner said work on the first 45m would be completed in 15 days. âSince work in OMR can be carried out only at night, it is causing a delay,â he said. Another major stormwater project is under way to divert excess water from the Arasankazhani canal to south Buckingham Canal and reduce pressure on Okkiyam Maduvu. This work too is expected to be completed within the next 20 days, Sameeran said. Last month, chief secretary M Sai Kumar directed all departments to complete northeast monsoon preparedness work by Sept 30.

body_clean: Chennai: Madras high court has categorically held that closure of a Tasmac shop located beyond the distance prescribed by law cannot be ordered by the court. However, it is open to Tamil Nadu govt to take an appropriate decision in accordance with law, the court said. Justice Hemanth Chandangoudar passed the order while disposing of a plea moved by T S Sridhar who wanted the court to direct Tasmac administration to close its shops at Sukurama Street, Parrys, Post Office Street, Prakasam Salai, Broadway (Near Mannady Metro), Jaffar Sarang Lane, opposite to Harbour and Wall Tax Road. The petitioner, represented by his counsel R S Raveendhren, said on the basis of govtâs policy decision to close retail liquor outlets situated within 500m of places of worship and educational institutions, he submitted a representation seeking closure of the Tasmac outlets in question. Opposing the plea, Tasmac said the outlets in question are beyond the prescribed distance from the places of worship and educational institutions. âSince the outlets are within the limits of a municipal corporation, the restriction under Rule 8(1) of the Tamil Nadu Liquor Retail Vending (in Shops and Bars) Rules, 2003, is not applicable,â he said. To this, Raveendhern said the policy decision is irrational since govt says that only 717 shops identified by it violate the norm of 500m, which has not been notified, and other shops in the state which are actually within 500m norm are not chosen for closure. Recording the submissions, the court said, âA division bench of this court has rejected a similar prayer, holding that no mandamus could be issued for closure of a Tasmac outlet when the outlet was situated beyond the prohibited distance prescribed under the applicable rules.â The bench further said that if the govt decides to change or revisit its policy, it is open to the govt to take an appropriate decision, the judge said, and disposed of the plea.

body_clean: Chennai: Terming it as demonstrably untenable, the Madras high court has dismissed a plea moved by âlegal heirsâ of former chief minister and founder of AIADMK M G Ramachandran seeking claim over a property in Virugambakkam. âThe administrator of the estate of the late M G Ramachandran, in the statement filed on Dec 14, 2023, has asserted that the petition-schedule property forms part of the property described in the Will as âSathya Garden,â situated in Saligramam and Virugambakkam and that it has vested in the M G R School and Home for the Speech and Hearing Impaired Trust,â Justice A D Maria Clete said. The court passed the order while dismissing a plea moved by late M C Ramamurthy, son of M G Chakrapani, brother of MGR and 14 others claiming to be Class II heirs of the former chief minister. In contrast, the earlier testamentary grant continues to operate,â the court added. The petitioners must pursue the remedy available to them in law before the appropriate forum. Unless the effect of the subsisting testamentary grant upon the property is displaced in proceedings recognised by law, no letters of administration based on intestate succession can be granted in respect of that property. Thus, viewed from any angle, the relief sought in the original petition is unsustainable, the court said.

title: HC orders framing of SOP for use of elephants in religious ceremonies
title_clean: HC orders framing of SOP for use of elephants in religious ceremonies
title_normalized: hc orders framing of sop for use of elephants in religious ceremonies
body_clean: Chennai: Asserting that the integration of captive animals into religious ceremonies cannot exist in a legal vacuum, the Madras high court has directed the Tamil Nadu govt to come up with a draft Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) governing the participation of elephants in religious functions and temple festivals. âElephants hold a significant place in the cultural, historical, and religious traditions of the state, where they participate in rituals and processions governed by ancient temple customs,â the first bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G Arul Murugan said. However, the integration of captive animals into religious ceremonies cannot exist in a legal vacuum; scriptural traditions must strictly accord with constitutional values, statutory safeguards, and the fundamental duty enjoined upon the state and citizens under Article 51A(g) of the Constitution to show compassion to living creatures, the court added. The court directed the state to constitute a joint working group comprising the chief wildlife warden, the commissioner of HR and CE, and expert veterinary officers. The working group shall draft and submit comprehensive, standardized governing, pre-festival health and microchip verification, transportation protocols, handler and mahout standards, and safety and environmental thresholds, the bench said. The court added that pending the finalisation and formal notification of the SOP, the officials shall ensure strict, unyielding compliance with the existing statutory provisions under the Wildlife (Protection) Act. Any violation of animal welfare standards or unapproved transportation during the pendency of these proceedings shall be met with immediate statutory action by the chief wildlife warden and the enforcement authorities, the judges said and adjourned the hearing to Oct 30. The court passed the interim order on a PIL moved by Seva Trust seeking formation of a SOP governing the participation of elephants in religious functions and temple festivals.

Consumption is unique, as households buy and stock crates of bottles,â a special bench of Justice N Sathish Kumar and Justice D Bharatha Chakravarthy said. Counterfeiting, including refilling, is another peculiar problem. Therefore, this is a grave and important concern for our country, and no comparison can be made with other countries, the court said while dismissing review applications moved by Food Safety and Standards Authority of India ( FSSAI ) seeking to review an order mandating such labels declaring presence of micro plastics in PET bottles and plastic packets in which sugar and salt are sold. âWe have already observed in our order dated Feb 6 that even placentas contain micro/nano plastics and that, if such particles cross the placenta and become part of the developing embryo, the situation is indeed grim,â the court said. The bench noted domestic and international studies and scientific literature been done with respect to the micro plasticsâ potential for affecting systems of digestive and gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, renal and excretory, reproductive developments, endocrine and metabolism, cellular and molecular and the possibility of long-term carcinogenic concerns. âAll studies confirm that these bio-non-degradable particles, once inside the body, pass through body barriers into the bloodstream and, as a contaminant, move through blood vessels into other organs,â the court said. The order mandating such labels is only the barest essential minimum, namely informing the consumer that the food may contain micro/nano plastics. We carefully considered the balance of convenience in our order and found that this is the barest essential minimum required at this stage, while the FSSAI proceeds with further enquiry relating to the risk assessment, the bench added.

summary_clean: The four new radars will be installed in Yercaud, Trichy, Kanyakumari and Ramanathapuram
body_clean: Chennai: The S-band Doppler weather radar at Chennai Port, which has been working for more than two decades, will be replaced in 2027 even as it has been restored and kept operational ahead of the Oct-Dec northeast monsoon. India Meteorological Department, in collaboration with the state govt, will install four new Doppler weather radars in interior Tamil Nadu to strengthen coverage. IMD director general of meteorology Mrutyunjay Mohapatra said an order to replace the ageing radar was placed six months ago. âThe existing one is fixed and is currently working. We can turn it on whenever we want. We will manage with it until we replace it,â he said. Imported from Germany, the Port radar has been operational since 2002 and has faced mechanical problems, including wear and tear in its antenna system and pedestal. Its bull gear, which rotates the antenna, had to be replaced, with Isro helping refurbish it as spare parts for the phased-out model were unavailable. The radar used to earlier be operated for a few hours when required because of these issues. The S-band radar has a range of about 500km and is important for tracking cyclones and other large weather systems, besides monitoring rain-bearing clouds. It provides information on rainfall structure, precipitation accumulation, wind speed and direction, cloud development and movement, and wind shear. A Doppler weather radar transmits electromagnetic waves and measures energy backscattered by water or ice particles in the atmosphere. Mohapatra said radars at Karaikal, Sriharikota and Thiruvananthapuram can provide coverage over Tamil Nadu if the Port radar fails, providing redundancy. The city also has an X-band radar at the NIOT campus in Pallikaranai, with a range of about 150km, used mainly for localised weather monitoring and nowcasting. âYou cannot assure that all radars will work well. Every time 30% radars will be down. There will be some problems. But we should have redundancy that we are ensuring,â he said. The four new radars will be installed in Yercaud, Trichy, Kanyakumari and Ramanathapuram, according to IMD. The expansion is part of a national plan to add 16 radars by March 2027, taking the network from 52 to 68, Mohapatra said. About 91% of the country is covered so far. âThe focus is on ensuring redundancy, while creating a denser radar network along the coast and strengthening coverage in hilly and urban areas,â he said.

body_clean: Chennai: What began as a de-addiction centre for students and employees who became increasingly dependent on the internet during the Covid-19 pandemic is now seeing senior citizens too seeking treatment for internet addiction, doctors at Omandurar Government Medical College Hospital said. Patients are advised to restrict social media use to 45 minutes a day, although doctors accept that it is difficult for families to distinguish between screen time spent on work or studies and time spent purely for entertainment. title: It’s Europe calling
title_clean: It’s Europe calling
title_normalized: it s europe calling
summary_clean: The Upcoming India-EU FTA Could Benefit Industries Across TN, Which Must Amp Up Exports
body_clean: Leading European countries are choosing Tamil Nadu for manufacturing plants and service-sector facilities to cater to global markets. Now, it is TNâs turn to scale up exports to Europe as the Free Trade Agreement (FTA) between India and European Union (EU) is likely to come into force early 2027. The EU has committed to eliminate duties on about 70.4% of tariff lines immediately, covering nearly 90.7% of Indiaâs export value, while another 20.3% of products will see phased tariff elimination. In total, the EUâs tariff concessions cover almost 97% of tariff lines and more than 99% of trade value. The agreement includes zero tariffs on leather, footwear, textiles, apparel, clothing and toys. Duties on several categories of motor vehicles, seafood, tyres, pumps, including injection pumps, and elevators will be eliminated. This puts TN in a strong position given its sectoral strengths. The FTA will improve EU market access, strengthening TNâs export competitiveness and integration into European value chains. Key sectors set to benefit include engineering goods, textiles and apparel, automobiles, pharma, ICT and financial services, leather, footwear, gems, jewellery, and rubber. FTAs give TN an opportunity to attract European investment and expand exports, but the bigger prize is moving from assembly to higher-value manufacturing, engineering and design. To capture it, TN needs stronger rules-of-origin support, carbon-compliance capabilities, global certification, specialised skills and incentives linked to value addition rather than capital deployed, said P Ravichandran, chairman, CII southern region. The upcoming trade deal has already enthused manufacturers. Recently, the Southern India Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SICCI) led a Tamil Nadu delegation for roadshows in Germany and Italy, showcasing opportunities in automotive, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, green mobility and skill development. V N Shiva Shankar, president, SICCI, said the roadshows received encouraging response from German business community. âA leading certification and standards group (second largest in Germany) came forward to establish a centre in Chennai to help SMEs leverage the FTA, especially with the carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) and other documentation. A leading semiconductor firm has committed to explore investments in Chennai, starting off first with contract manufacturing and then moving on to setting up their own units,â he said. Of the total $59.3bn merchandise exports from TN in 2025â26, EU countries accounted for roughly $11.3bn (about 19%). The FTAâs services and digital-trade provisions, along with improved regulatory transparency, professional mobility and SME support, are also relevant to TNâs IT/ITeS, GCC, professional and financial-services ecosystem. âExporters should use this to adopt demand-driven, country-specific market strategies, and strengthen EU regulatory/compliance readiness. SICCI proposes to establish an IndiaâEU FTA Desk in Chennai as a dedicated support mechanism for TN exporters, MSMEs, investors, and industry associations. The desk will provide a single point of reference for EU market intelligence, market access data, compliance norms, investment facilitation and policy advocacy, helping businesses translate the FTA into actionable opportunities. We propose to establish this in Dec 2026 as a part of the chamberâs exports facilitation,â he added. Ahead of the FTA between India and EU, a delegation from SICCI organised a series of roadshows in Germany and Italy Raja M Shanmugam, former president of Tirupur Exporters Association, said Tirupur exported garments worth close to $2bn to the EU in FY26, accounting for about 37% of its total exports. Germany, France, Italy, Scandinavian countries and Poland are top destinations, with products including sweat jackets, T-shirts, polo T-shirts and sportswear. Noting that the FTA could be a game changer for Tirupur and similar clusters, he said India is at a disadvantage because Bangladesh, Vietnam, Cambodia and Sri Lanka have zero-tariff access to the EU. âAgainst this backdrop, the upcoming FTA will eliminate the 10% tariff on textiles for exports from India to the EU. This has the potential to double Tirupurâs exports to $4 billion in value terms and increase the volume by 1.5 times to the EU over the next four years,â he said. Israr Ahmed, former vice-president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO) and MD of Farida Group, said, âOnce in force, we expect footwear exports from TN to the EU to grow by at least 15%-20%. This growth would also help Indian exporters reduce their reliance on the US market, particularly given the ongoing risk of further US tariff increases.â Mohamed Athif, secretary, Seafood Exporters Association of India, Tamil Nadu Region, said the EU is one of the largest markets for frozen cephalopods such as squid, octopus and cuttlefish from Tamil Nadu. The upcoming IndiaâEU FTA is expected to significantly boost exports.

title_clean: Now, Tasmac employees can’t cite maintenance expenses for collecting additional money from liquor buyers
title_normalized: now tasmac employees can t cite maintenance expenses for collecting additional money from liquor buyers
summary_clean: Tasmac liquor shops to get up to Rs 5,000 a month to improveupkeep
body_clean: CHENNAI: Liquor buyers can hope for tidier and better-maintained Tasmac shops soon. The state-run liquor retailer is enhancing the monthly maintenance provision for its outlets by nearly seven times, from the existing Rs 750 to up to Rs 5,000, as part of a series of welfare measures aimed at improving the working atmosphere for employees and providing a more pleasant experience for buyers. The new provision will come into effect on Oct 1, according to a circular issued by Tasmac managing director K Nanthakumar on Sept 29. The monthly petty-cash system, which has been in place since 2003 for meeting minor day-to-day expenses at retail shops, will now be replaced by the higher maintenance allocation. The move was among the welfare measures announced by prohibition and excise minister K Vignesh in the Tamil Nadu assembly on Aug 31. It comes after Tasmac revised the salaries of retail shop employees with effect from Sept 1 and announced an annual Rs 6,000 allowance towards three sets of uniforms, besides a Rs 20,000 festival advance. The latest measure is significant in the backdrop of persistent complaints of Tasmac personnel charging buyers more than the maximum retail price (MRP). Maintenance expenses have been cited by workers as one of the reasons for collecting additional amounts from liquor buyers. The govt has, meanwhile, warned that employees found violating MRP norms would face suspension and dismissal for repeat offences. Under the revised system, shops in corporation areas will receive Rs 5,000 a month, those in municipalities and town panchayats Rs 4,000 and those in rural and village panchayat areas Rs 3,000. The amount will be credited every month along with the salary of the shop supervisor. For October, the maintenance amount is to be released on Sept 30 along with the September salary. The funds are to be used primarily for keeping the shops clean. Supervisors can spend them on daily cleaning of the shop premises, counter area and immediate surroundings, besides buying brooms, cleaning agents, disinfectants, phenyl, waste bins, garbage bags and other cleaning consumables. The allocation can also be used to provide drinking water, including purchase of water cans, hiring or maintenance of a water dispenser or pot and the cost of drinking water. Other basic amenities required for employees and consumers can also be provided from the funds. The money, however, cannot be used for shop rent, electricity charges, building repairs, furniture, equipment, capital items or expenditure for which a separate provision exists. The supervisor will be responsible for maintaining a monthly expenditure register and preserving bills, vouchers and receipts for three years. The records will be subject to inspection by district managers and internal or statutory auditors. Tasmac has approved a 5% annual indexation of the maintenance provision, with the revised amount to be rounded to the nearest Rs 100. The first revision will take effect on April 1, 2027, with the revised rates to be notified by the head office each year.

title: Plant based menus take seed at colleges
title_clean: Plant based menus take seed at colleges

body_clean: Canteens are increasingly adding recipes without meat, fish or dairy products. Student chefs at SRM Institute of Hotel Management Starting 2027, future chefs at SRM Institute of Hotel Management in Kattankulathur will spend a fifth of their coursework learning to cook without meat, fish, eggs or dairy. The institute has also cut animal products in its dining halls and hostels by 30%, as part of a growing push for plant-based food on Indian campuses. The institution recently collaborated with Humane World for Animals India, which sent professionals to campus to train faculty in plant-based food preparation. âIt covered the fundamentals of plant-based cooking, ingredient substitution, menu planning and preparation of dishes without meat, fish, eggs and dairy products,â says Lalitha Shri, vice principal. âWe reduced animal products in campus dining and hostels to align practical dining hall practices with classroom learning.â They are not the only ones. Pondicherry University serves plant-based food in its campus canteens and hostels on Tuesdays, so does Bharath Institute of Higher Education and Research (BIHER), Chennai. The German International School in Chennai, one of the first to make a move in this direction, had announced in 2017 that they would serve 100% plant-based meals to their students and avoid using animal products on campus. At BITS Pilani, Hyderabad, there is a separate vegan counter within the mess, says Parth Gupta, a third year student, and joint secretary of the Club for Animal Rights and Equality. âIn our case, nearly half the mess menu was plant-based. It took some time to convince the administration, but eventually they agreed to introduce such an alternative. The mess vendors were willing to prepare vegan alternatives for curries with milk or other dairy products such as soya chunks or cashew-based cream,â says Parth. In India, especially in South India, much of vegetarian food is plant-based. However, turning a govt institutionâs canteen plant-based is still problematic owing to the political colours it might take on, says Naman Dedhia, of the organisation Plant Based Treaty, which works with educational institutions across the world to teach them about plant-based cuisine. âBut there is definitely a movement among private institutions in India.â The dishes are not as bland or unappetising as many imagine, says Sheetal Ahuja, director of Vision International School of Excellence, Ankleshwar, Gujarat, where the canteen went vegan three years ago. âWe worked closely with a nutritionist and put a lot of thought into the menu. We experimented with different combinations and cuisines to ensure that the children received good sources of protein, essential amino acids, fibre and other nutrients.â In order to not make children feel that something had been taken away from them, they adapted familiar foods. âWe marinated tofu to give it a paneer-like texture. We introduced soy curd, soy lassi, almond milk, kheer and several other nutritious and tasty desserts,â she says. âWe talk to children about the compassion behind these choices. Many of them are happy that in their own small way, they can contribute to creating a better world for animals.â At SRM, the practical sessions exposed students to ingredients such as vegetables, fruits, grains, pulses, legumes, nuts, seeds, coconut and plant-based dairy alternatives. Students learn how familiar dishes can be recreated using plant-based ingredients while retaining flavour, texture, presentation and nutritional value. âThe focus is also on techniques rather than recipes. Students are encouraged to understand how ingredients behave, how flavour can be developed using herbs and spices, how plant proteins can be incorporated into menus, and how locally available produce can be used creatively,â says Lalitha Shri. âVegan cuisine is not simply about removing animal-based ingredients; it is about reimagining food with creativity, nutrition and sustainability at its heart. The future of hospitality lies in creating food that is delicious, innovative and mindful of both people and the planet.â While plant-based diets are beneficial for the gut and are fibre-rich, Vitamin B12 deficiencies are often not found, which might have to be addressed through supplements, says Mumtaz Khalid Ismael, consultant clinical dietician. âThere are also significant environmental benefits,â says Sridhar A, environmental researcher. âIntroducing more plant-based meals in schools and colleges as a dietary choice, is an opportunity to reduce the environmental footprint of the food system while shaping sustainable and ethical habits among young people. Food systems contribute more than one third of global greenhouse gas emissions, and evidence shows that diets with less animal-based food can substantially reduce pressures on land, water, biodiversity and climate.â Beyond health and environmental concerns, there is the ethical question, says Sai Vignesh, vegan advocate and founder of the Chennai-based organisation Almighty Animal Care Trust. âIf human beings can thrive on a plant-based diet, why should we continue consuming animals? I would say the ethical aspect should remain at the forefront.â

And Veeramani steps out only to pick up a newspaper kept beneath a small stone and return to his room. Being an A-class inmate, Veeramani has been accommodated in a room larger than a regular prison cell. He has also been provided with a bed and chair and permitted to receive a newspaper of his choice. Veeramani preferred an English business daily. title: Record-high breeding for non-native birds at Pallikaranai marshland

title_normalized: record high breeding for non native birds at pallikaranai marshland
body_clean: Chennai: From the long-legged bronze-winged Jacanas to fulvous whistling ducks and pied mynas, non-native birds found predominantly in parts of south and north India have had a healthy start to the migratory season at Pallikaranai this year with record breeding. For instance, the Jacanas â which had vanished from the marshland for decades before reappearing in single digits in 2014 â were found in the hundreds this month. In fact, 185 Jacanas were sighted in Sept and 201 in Aug; the highest-ever count for the bird since its reappearance. As for the fulvous whistling ducks, a record 1,155 birds were found in the marshland in Sept, an exponential increase from just 68 birds recorded in the same month last year. Further, 40 pied mynas, with at least 23 hatchlings, were found by birders this month . âIt is one thing for Pallikaranaiâs native birds to breed in such huge numbers, but truly special for non-native birds to be found in such huge numbers. This indicates a favourable habitat for these birds,â said K V R K Thirunaranan, founder of The Nature Trust. Birders say floating vegetation, coupled with organic waste, may have created a conducive habitat for these birds. âFulvous whistling ducks and jacanas love to be near floating vegetation. Additionally, the presence of sewage in the marshland creates organic waste, which attracts worms,â Thirunaranan added. Domestic cattle, too, help flush out prey for pied mynas. Forest officials say draining of water from the marshland could have helped too. âWe have 12 guards at the marshland, who monitor the site round-the-clock to prevent poaching and make the atmosphere safe for the birds,â said V A Saravanan, Chennai district forest officer.

The stretch, from the eastern entrance of Tambaram railway station to Camp Road junction, has remained riddled with patches and potholes for more than three months. The road, originally around 80ft wide, is now reduced to about 40ft of usable carriageway at several points, with the remaining portion either dug up for underground sewerage works or reduced to a mud-and-sand surface. The road is a key link between GST Road and Velachery, passing through Medavakkam and Pallikaranai, and carries around 1,000 vehicles per hour. The ongoing work involves constructing underground sewerage connections to areas including Selaiyur, Valmiki Street, and interior parts of Chromepet. âEvery day, at least 10 bikers skid and fall due to the uneven surface. Metrowater officials said underground sewerage work had not stalled and that 75% of the work has been completed. The remaining work is expected to be finished by mid-Oct. body_clean: Chennai: Residents of Nehru Ninaivu Nagar, Royapuram, have urged Greater Chennai Corporation and police to install CCTV cameras at key locations in the locality, citing a spate of crimes, including chain-snatching and murder . Locals said the absence of cameras has left several areas vulnerable, with no visible steps taken to strengthen surveillance. âRecently, there were two crime cases in the area. After multiple complaints, police took up the cases, but there were no steps taken to move the investigations forward. Several cases remain unsolved because there is no usable footage,â said Ajith Kumar, a resident of Nehru Ninaivu Nagar. Residents said the absence of cameras has left them feeling vulnerable, especially women, children and those returning home late at night. They said the lack of CCTV cameras has contributed to an increase in anti-social activities in the locality at night. Police patrols too have become less frequent in the neighbourhood, they added. The police, however, said the locality had not witnessed any major crime recently. Royapuram N1 law and order inspector S Anbukarasan said, âThe locality has reported less than 10 cases, with nothing major such as murder. If residents want to install CCTV cameras, they can contribute money and install them. Otherwise, GCC can also them,â he said. âWe no longer feel safe on our streets after dark. The authorities cannot wait for a serious incident to happen before taking action. Cameras must be installed in vulnerable stretches immediately to ensure accountability and improve safety,â said J Kamalesh, a resident. When contacted, Royapuram zonal officer N Sathyanarayanan said, âSteps will be taken by police to install CCTV cameras based on the requirements of the locality. If residents raise any complaints, we will intimate the department concerned.â

body_clean: CHENNAI: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has arrested two absconding accused in the HashPe cryptocurrency fraud case, in which people were duped of more than Rs 146 crore on the promise of high returns if they invested in a cryptocurrency named TCX. The accused, identified as Syed Usman alias Babu and Dhamodharan Balachandran of Coimbatore, were produced before the special court for PMLA cases in Chennai on Tuesday and were remanded in judicial custody. Earlier, ED arrested Hitesh Kumar and Imran Basha from Coimbatore on Sept 1 after carrying out searches in 11 places in Chennai, Coimbatore and Kolkata in connection with the fraud. ED initiated investigations under PMLA based on an FIR registered by the CB-CID, Puducherry, in which the victims had alleged that they had been cheated in the guise of an investment scheme floated by the accused. After all passengers boarded and the aircraft began moving towards the runway, the pilot detected an engine problem and stopped the aircraft. He added that the cityâs two desalination plants are meeting requirements of the city. A third desalination plant, with a capacity of 450 MLD, is under construction and is expected to become operational by March next year. The official said dependence on reservoirs could fall once it is commissioned. Despite the shortfall, Metrowater expressed confidence that Chennai would not face a situation like the 2018 crisis. The picture is grimmer outside the piped network. I Annadurai of Thangam Bore Wells said the groundwater table has dried up in several localities, particularly in the southern and western parts of the city beyond Guindy, where Metrowater supply is patchy. title: Tambaram’s ₹2,000-cr revenue opportunity in tatters

body_clean: In Tambaram, a commercial building springs up, another floor is added to a house and a vacant stretch along a busy road turns into a parking lot almost every month. Yet much of this does not show up in the revenue records. Five years after it was upgraded from a Chennai suburban municipality to a corporation, Tambaramâs revenue increase has been lukewarm, as the civic body has not expanded its tax and non-tax revenue base smartly. An analysis by TOI shows that outdoor advertising, property tax reassessment, arrear recovery, professional tax and regulated parking could together raise the corporationâs annual revenue from around â11,447 crore in 2026-27 to about â12,000 crore in the next fiscal. Once a 20.7sqkm municipality, it now covers about 85sqkm across five zones and 70 wards, with a population of nearly 10 lakh. Even so, property records have not kept pace. The records show 2.3 lakh assessed properties based on a 2019 assessment. âAt least 1.5 lakh more buildings have come up after Covid. But only a handful of people register changes and get confirmation from the civic body before construction,â said D S Sivasamy, former additional director of municipal administration and water supply department. He said local-level monitoring has also weakened. âA decade ago, a register was managed by corporations to keep track of new buildings. No such register exists now,â he said. Property tax could be the biggest source of additional revenue, a senior corporation official said. Of the assessed properties, only 42.4% of owners pay their tax in full. The civic body also has a large pool of arrears, running up to â1200 crore. The proportion of annual taxpayers increased from 56% in 2023-24 to 58.2% in 2025-26. Experts say a fresh assessment could increase the number of assessed properties to around four lakh, generating â1100 crore more revenue. âRecently, the property taxes were increased from â1414 a year to â14,760 in some areas without prior notice. If a property has been assessed, how can the tax be revised? They should collect taxes from defaulters rather than increasing the burden on those who pay,â said S Jayaram from East Tambaram. Outdoor advertising is another largely untapped source. Tambaram has only 84 authorised ad spaces, generating â11.26 crore annually. It has around 580 roads and 51 bus shelters. At least 100 unauthorised billboards operate at prominent stretches. The monthly advertising rate is â14,500 per sqm. A 30sqm billboard fetches at least â11.35 lakh per month. Better use of billboards, bus shelters, medians and other spaces could increase the ad income to â150 crore annually. Commercial establishments in areas such as Radial Road and West Tambaram have converted vacant spaces into parking areas. At least one lakh vehicles pass through the stretch daily. A regulated policy, with a parking complex, could generate up to â184 crore annually. Professional tax also remains under-assessed. At present, 1,22,384 salaried professionals contribute about â140 crore. The corporation now gets about â185 crore from vacant land tax, profession tax, water charges, sewerage charges, UGSS and other non-tax revenue. Better assessment and collection could raise this pool to â1156 crore. R Saranya, the civic body commissioner, said they had begun steps to improve collections. âWe sent notices to defaulters and gave them time till the end of this month to pay up. We are working to resolve the issue of increased taxes in a few localities,â she said.

title: Tamil Nadu’s next leap must prioritise speed over subsidies

body_clean: BY INVITATIONTamil Nadu has long been one of Indiaâs economic paradoxes. It combines high levels of industrialisation with expansive welfare commitments, robust manufacturing with social development, and fiscal stress with investor enthusiasm. The new govtâs challenge is not to create growth from scratch, but to accelerate an already-running growth machine without letting the gears of public finance grind themselves down. A survey of 65 CFOs conducted by KPMG, knowledge partner to the CFO Board, and supplemented by interviews and discussions with several other finance leaders in TN, offers a glimpse into what businesses want. The findings are encouraging. Capital availability is not the central constraint: 92% said access to growth capital was not a barrier, more than three-fourths expected fresh capital expenditure in TN, and two-thirds foresaw inorganic growth opportunities. The obstacle is not a lack of investor appetite, but the quality and speed of execution. The survey finds that only 39% of respondents rate the stateâs ease of doing business as better than that of competing states. The report benchmarks the state against the faster approval frameworks of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, while recognising TNâs relatively stable and dependable business environment. Their recommendation is straightforward: simplify approvals, expand self-certification, adopt deemed approvals after specified timelines, and provide dedicated relationship managers for major investments. Although the recent state budget has struck the right note with Guidance 3.0, Single Window Portal 3.0 and AI-enabled approval systems, the larger challenge is administrative and cultural. Businesses will change their assessment only when they consistently experience faster, more predictable approvals on the ground. The surveyâs second message is equally striking: 85% of CFOs identified attracting and retaining talent as a key priority. This suggests that TNâs competitiveness over the next decade will depend as much on liveability as on industrial policy. Better housing, transport, healthcare, schools and urban amenities could prove as important as industrial parks and incentives. This is particularly relevant for Chennai. The city already has strong educational institutions and a large industrial ecosystem. Yet talent competition is becoming both national and global. For internationally mobile professionals, Chennai increasingly competes not only with Bengaluru and Hyderabad, but also with global business destinations. This raises the premium on housing, mobility, urban amenities, and cosmopolitan appeal. Infrastructure is the third recurring theme. CFOs highlighted connectivity, logistics, airports, public transport and digital infrastructure as critical to growth, with faster metro projects, better transport integration, stronger industrial-cluster logistics and Chennai airport upgrades among key priorities. The broader message is clear: Chennai and other key cities must become more convenient, liveable and cosmopolitan to attract more global capability centres, technology firms and multinational investment. Perhaps the most interesting finding concerns artificial intelligence. Corporate leaders are not chasing futuristic possibilities. They want AI to improve productivity, manufacturing efficiency, customer experience and back-office automation. This pragmatic approach aligns well with the stateâs industrial strengths and offers a path to higher productivity without abandoning the stateâs manufacturing foundation. The broad message emerging from the report is refreshingly practical. Tamil Nadu does not need a dramatic reinvention. It already has the ingredients for success: an economy projected to exceed â140 lakh crore in 2026â27, a deep industrial base, strong human capital and significant investor interest. What it needs is relentless execution: faster approvals, stronger infrastructure, greater fiscal discipline, and policies that turn talent into productivity. In economics, growth miracles rarely come from grand announcements. They come from doing ordinary things exceptionally well. Tamil Naduâs next leap may depend less on setting new ambitions and more on delivering those already articulated. (The author is the office managing partner, Chennai, KPMG in India)

summary_clean: Keep Fort St George, or move the complex only as the anchor of a compact, vertical, climate-resilient satellite city, not as another isolated govt enclave
body_clean: K Ashok Vardhan Shetty For a quarter-century, successive govts have sought to relocate Tamil Nadu âs secretariat from Fort St George. Every proposal provoked controversy and was eventually abandoned; even the one completed complex was repurposed into a multi-speciality hospital. The secretariat is best retained at Fort St George. Its congestion-related drawbacks are outweighed by its central location, excellent transport connectivity, and proximity to the principal govt directorates. All your fears will vanish.â The relationship Tamilvanan, with his signature hat and dark glasses, a curious blend of Tamil assertion and Western styling, forged with his readers, young and old, and his enormous confidence in his own public persona as an author and editor, are reflected in that answer. His self-assurance rested on his faith in the effectiveness of his writing, rooted in a native intelligence and a gift for lucid exposition. In his centenary year, many of those readers, particularly the ones who found him while still at school, remember the man and his magazine for his slogan, âThunive Thunaiâ (Courage is our companion), and for introducing them to the habit â and the pleasure â of reading. Through this colourful journalistic persona and the crisp writing in âKalkanduâ, the magazine he edited from its founding in 1948, he held the attention of a vast readership for more than a quarter of a century, until his premature death in 1977. The headmaster of a respected English-medium school who subscribed to âKalkanduâ was surprised to discover that his aged mother had become an admirer of Tamilvanan for the clarity with which he explained the concepts of the Bhagavad Gita to his readers. When the impact of his public image is considered alongside his journalistic instinct, one gets a sense of the Tamilvanan phenomenon of the early decades of the 1950s. A real-life incident illustrates the point: two muggers who had waylaid him fled in the mistaken belief that he was a policeman in plain clothes, after being rattled by his loud, uproarious laughter. After a brief stint as a helper and assistant on the Pudukkottai-based Tamil monthly âPonniâ, in 1944, Tamilvanan joined âGrama Oozhiyanâ, published from Thuraiyur near Trichy, as a sub-editor. Its proprietor was A V R Krishnaswami Reddiar; Vallikkannan was its editor. It was here that Tamilvanan became fascinated by the lucid prose of N Pichamoorthy (considered the father of free verse in Tamil), particularly his use of short sentences to explain things simply. Reddiar came to know of the young sub-editorâs admiration for Pichamoorthyâs writing and one day took him to meet the writer, who lived in a small house at Chettikulam near Thuraiyur. Introducing Tamilvanan, Reddiar told Pichamoorthy: âHere is your rasika.â Pichamoorthy received the young admirer with affection. âThambi,â he told him, âalways write in a simple style. Avoid long sentences. Do this and one day you too will become a renowned writer.â Some time after this meeting, Vallikkannan left âGrama Oozhiyanâ, and Tamilvanan became its editor. He remained there for about three-and-a-half years, until the magazine folded. He then proceeded to Chennai, where, under the guidance of the seminal Tamil publisher and editor âSaktiâ Vai Govindan, he edited âAnilâ, a childrenâs magazine. In the city, he teamed up with schoolmate Tirunavukkarasu, who later helmed the prestigious âVanathi Pathippagamâ, and together they published books for children under the âJil Jilâ imprint. The reprints of the cheaply priced Tamilvanan-authored titles impressed printer P V Parthasarathy so much that he recommended him to his partner, S A P Annamalai, editor of Kumudam. That recommendation led to the birth of âKalkanduâ as a sister publication of âKumudamâ. Under Tamilvanan, the 32-page âKalkanduâ became so famous that âKumudamâ was advertised on its back wrapper with the words: âHave you read Kumudam?â Kumudamâs editor SAP recognised that Tamilvanan was inseparable from the identity of Kalkandu. He beautifully summed up Tamilvananâs relationship with the magazine to his sub editors: ââThere is no Kalkandu without the personality of Tamilvanan. Just as Mother India sells because of its editor Baburao Patel and Blitz for R K Karanjia, Kalkandu sells on the force of Tamilvananâs personalityââ! While SAP and Tamilvanan shared mutual respect, the latter would call upon SAP in the office only rarely and speak to him for only a few minutes. It is said that SAP would marvel at Tamilvananâs animated conversation and dynamism. Once when SAP was downcast because of a new bus stop outside the gate of the office which was causing a lot of inconvenience to his employees, Tamilvanan is said to have driven straight to the police commissionerâs office and instantly had it shifted! Tamilvanan also proved successful as a fiction writer in the genre of detective novels. He created the character Sankarlal, the Tamilised version of Sherlock Holmes, and had him work out his skills of detection in exotic countries and climes, marshalling to good effect the knowledge of various foreign locations he had gained during his wide travels. Tamilvanan had even written a book on how to live to a hundred. Sadly, he lived to just cross fifty. Yet, in an extraordinary continuation of his legacy, his elder son Lena Tamilvanan carried on his fatherâs work as editor of Kalkandu for more than four decades after his untimely death, while his younger son Ravi Tamilvanan has expanded the publishing house. â MASTER OF ALLâ Ramanathan of Devakottai, while learning Tamil under the savant Thiru Vi Ka, came across the word âVaananâ and named himself Tamilvanan with the latterâs approval Made and sold products like âTamil Toothpowderâ and medicinal oils for shoulder pain and joint pain Established a publishing house in the name of his wife Manimekalai. With the reputation of being a âmaster of all subjectsâ, he wrote books on a wide range of subjects which sold well In the pushback against Ma Po Siâs glorification of Kattabomman in the 1950s and early 1960s, Tamilvanan portrayed the Poligar as a plundering dacoit Tried his hand in the world of films, dubbing six other-language films into Tamil. He wrote the story and dialogues and produced âKaadhalikka Vaangaâ (1972); it was his last (The writer has authored several books on cinema)

But that is a different question from saying that a governor can never obtain independent legal advice. Article 165 creates the office of the advocate general for the state. It provides that the governor shall appoint a person qualified to be a high court judge as advocate general. Article 165(2) provides that it is the advocate generalâs duty to advise the govt of the state on legal matters and to perform such other duties of a legal character as may from time to time be referred or assigned to him by the governor. That unquestionably establishes the constitutional position of the advocate general. But where is the prohibition? Article 165 does not say that the advocate general is the exclusive legal adviser of the governor. Nor does it say that a governor confronted with a difficult constitutional question concerning his own office is legally barred from obtaining another professional opinion. A power to refer legal duties to the advocate general is not necessarily the same thing as an exclusive obligation to refer every legal question to him. If the Constitution intended to impose an exclusivity rule of such significance, one would ordinarily expect some textual or structural indication of it; that indication is not readily apparent in Article 165. The advocate general can advise the governor. The governor can seek another opinion. This is where the distinction between constitutional office and professional legal advice becomes critical. A private lawyer consulted by the governor does not thereby become a constitutional authority. He cannot exercise the governorâs powers or make decisions under Article 200. He cannot summon the council of ministers or reserve a bill for the consideration of the President. He cannot perform the constitutional functions of the governor. He can only advise. The governor decides. What if the governor and the state govt take different legal views? The governor ordinarily functions on the aid and advice of the council of ministers, subject to those situations in which the Constitution requires or permits the governor to exercise a distinct constitutional judgment. Consider a situation in which the governor is required to determine the constitutional limits of his own office while the state govt takes a different legal position. The question is not whether the advocate general is a competent lawyer. The narrower question is: Does the Constitution compel the governor, whenever he seeks legal advice, to obtain it only from the advocate general? Govts routinely obtain professional advice from lawyers, consultants, experts and specialists under executive or administrative arrangements, subject to applicable law, financial rules and constitutional limitations. The real questions are, therefore: What exactly has been created? By what authority? With what functions? And at whose expense? If public money is spent, and facilities provided, there must be lawful authority for that expenditure. If confidential state material is shared, appropriate safeguards must exist. But they do not, by themselves, establish a general constitutional rule that the governor can never consult an independent lawyer. The Keralam experience is worth examining; not as a constitutional precedent, but as evidence that the proposition is not self-evident in constitutional practice. Keralam has an advocate general and other state law officers, yet there have been instances in which the governor has had access to separate legal advice. That practice, by itself, does not establish constitutional validity. But neither can it simply be ignored. Article 163 must also be handled carefully. The governor is not a free-standing constitutional act or entitled to disregard the elected govt whenever he chooses. The constitutional scheme makes aid and advice the general rule, subject to the limited situations in which the Constitution requires or permits a different exercise of judgment. But that principle does not answer the separate question of who may provide legal advice to the governor. He does not. The point is narrower: The governor may sometimes need to understand independently what the Constitution permits him to do. The strongest objection to a particular appointment, therefore, may not be that Article 165 automatically prohibits an independent legal adviser. The stronger constitutional questions are whether the arrangement: Creates a new public office without lawful authority Duplicates the advocate generalâs constitutionally assigned functions Bypasses applicable financial or administrative rules Gives access to public resources without proper authority Purports to confer powers that the Constitution has not given the adviser Those objections can and should be tested. The advocate general is the stateâs constitutional law officer, that office must be respected and its constitutional functions preserved. But preserving the constitutional position of the advocate general does not necessarily require converting Article 165 into a prohibition against every other form of professional legal advice. The Constitution creates offices. It does not create monopolies unless the constitutional text or necessary implication requires it. The debate should therefore be framed more precisely. Candidates urge the state govt to make Teachers Recruitment Board into a competent and autonomous recruitment body. âThe descriptive-type questions should be asked from their relevant subjects instead of general topics. Further, the state govt should video record the entire interview process to rule out any malpractices,â said S Swaminathan, adviser to the NET SLET Association.
