title: Chennai port system to ease container movement
title_clean: Chennai port system to ease container movement
title_normalized: chennai port system to ease container movement
body_clean: CHENNAI: Chennai Port Authority has launched a digital system ‘Port Setu’ to track export containers on the road between inland warehouses and the port gate. It is the first step towards making gate entry fully paperless. Port Setu, uses automatic number plate recognition, optical character recognition and RFID readers, linked to the customs ICEGATE platform. It records the time each trailer takes to travel from a container freight station (CFS) to the port. The system, developed by the Chennai chapter of the National Association of Container Freight Stations (NACFS), went live on September 17 and was formally launched on Wednesday. It forms the first phase of an Intelligent Vehicle Monitoring System (IVMS) being implemented under the central government’s One Nation One Port Process (ONOP) initiative to standardise and digitise procedures across Indian ports. For the freight stations, the main promise is more efficient use of trucks. Port Setu gives them real-time visibility of trailer arrivals at the port. The authority expects this to cut turnaround times and allow one extra round trip for every six made. The next phase is expected to take the system closer to a paperless port gate. Under Phase 2 of the IVMS, the container terminals will digitise the verification of seal intactness, a release stated. Sachin S Kurve, chairperson of Chennai Port Authority, said the system would provide greater visibility of container movement and help CFSs optimise trailer management.

Meanwhile, the police have intensified the probe and are investigating multiple angles and leads, including ‘financial transactions’ that allegedly led to the case being suppressed in the past and a land deal involving highly influential people to prevent legal action. Veeramani, the prime suspect, and his accomplices – Shanthi and her husband Mahendra Simhan (63) who allegedly facilitated the offence – were booked under Sections 7, 8, 15(1) and 21(1) of the Pocso Act and Section 67 of the Information Technology Act. They were arrested in August this year, 11 months after the case was registered. Speaking at an event here on Monday, Law Minister CTR Nirmal Kumar compared the allegations against Veeramani with the Pollachi sexual assault case and questioned how the matter could allegedly be diluted or escape immediate scrutiny when the police department was under the control of then CM M K Stalin. Nirmal Kumar questioned why the case did not receive immediate attention and sought an explanation from the previous government over the handling of the allegations. School Education Minister A Rajmohan questioned the Left parties’ stand on the case, asking whether they condemned the alleged suppression of the case. Alleging that the previous regime had allowed political interference in the police department, PWD Minister Aadhav Arjuna claimed that different standards of policing were applied based on political connections.

body_clean: CHENNAI: Responding to the accessibility issues for elderly and persons with disabilities at Tambaram Railway Station, highlighted by TNIE in its report on September 20, the Southern Railway said that porters have been instructed not to carry passengers on luggage trolleys and instead use wheelchairs. They have also been asked to not charge beyond the prescribed rate. Southern Railway said that 13 wheelchairs have been stationed at various locations within the station. For elderly, who may need assistance for wheelchair, the prescribed railway charges of `100 will apply. Wheelchairs are also provided to passengers to assist their accompanying elderly passengers, upon submission of any valid identification document to station master. The document is retained as a security measure and returned to passengers upon safe return of the wheelchair. For persons with disabilities, wheelchair assistance has been provided free of cost. Other assistance facilities, including offering support in accompanying wheelchair users up to the train and facilitating their boarding, will be available on a temporary basis until the new Foot Over Bridge is commissioned, a railway official said. Information regarding prescribed porter charges, assistance contact number, porter services, wheelchair availability and dedicated contact number have been displayed at prominent locations within the station. Those who need wheelchair can contact the number, or the station manager or station master for availing it, the official added. On concerns that the trolley path and the ramp to access the platforms are difficult to navigate in wheelchairs, officials said that work is ongoing to smoothen the pathway and make it user-friendly, and that it will be completed in one or two days. They added that the pathway is usable with an escort.

body_clean: CHENNAI: After facing an uproar from councillors over pending ward development funds at its last council meeting, the Greater Chennai Corporation on Thursday announced the first instalment of Rs 30 lakh each, half the annual allocation, a day before the council meets again on Friday. Some councillors had even threatened to resign unless the funds were released. The first instalment for 2026-27 totals Rs 60.6 crore for 200 elected councillors and two nominated councillors representing persons with disabilities. The corporation has asked zonal officers to obtain recommendations from councillors for works ahead of the northeast monsoon, according to a release from GCC. title: Material Memoir: Chennai artists explore memory through transformed materials
title_clean: Material Memoir: Chennai artists explore memory through transformed materials
title_normalized: material memoir chennai artists explore memory through transformed materials
summary_clean: At Artiform, Mylapore, the exhibition brings together artists Kannan P, Mani Murugesan, Ramki Ravi, Ramesh N, Surya S, and Yogeshwaran V who explores how wood, metal, graphite, and paper become materials for storytelling
body_clean: Our understanding of the world around us is constantly shaped by the materials that fill it. For artists, this relationship can become part of the creative process. In Material Memoir, a new show at Artiform, Mylapore, substances like wood, metal, and graphite, move beyond their physical forms to become ways of telling stories. Carved, layered, cut, shaped, each material gradually becomes a part of a narrative. The audience is left to wonder whether materials can indeed remember. The exhibition brings together the works of upcoming Chennai-based artists Kannan P, Mani Murugesan, Ramki Ravi, Ramesh N, Surya S and Yogeshwaran V. Some pieces quickly announce the idea of contemplating material memory and the central nature of life through indents, and suspension. There are some others that show you the palpable changes taking place in Nature through nests and webs. Take Kannan’s practice, for instance. He evidently engages with welding, sheet metal, wood, and bronze. Welding is central to his visual language. One of his pieces titled Metallic Nest: Solitude and Synergy, made entirely with steel, is inspired by the “collective architecture of the wasp’s nest,” says Kannan. Growing up in Chennai’s Ambattur, the presence of a wasp’s nest is something that he witnessed often. “A single paper wasp or honeybee cannot build a hive alone, yet together they craft complex structures through collective labour. In my practice and in life, I believe true strength and beauty emerge not from isolated creation, but from shared unity,” says Kannan. “Every time I clean a spider’s web in my house, it rebuilds again and again. Watching this cycle sparked a deep personal realisation. No matter how many times its creation is disrupted, the spider stays focussed solely on its work. For me, this only means that I need to keep moving forward despite every obstacle or setback. That is what I have tried to do in Perseverance,” he adds. Kannan says that the way he has used steel to construct a suspended human takes the form of a spider’s home and its infinite web. The piece, an already striking visual, hence becomes that much more compelling. “We think of wood, graphite, paper, metal, and all these materials as just something that is used to create an artwork. But when you actually look closely, they are not just materials. That is where the story begins. Each artist has approached the material in a different way, and even though their styles are distinctive, the material they have used carries an evocation,” says curator Isaiarasi Annamalai. Forms of Nature There are other artists who seem to be gravitating towards hymenoptera, arachnids, and other small creatures. Artist Ramki Ravi transforms paper through cutting, carving, and layering, challenging the material’s inherent flatness. Inspired by the forms of Nature, the sculpted pieces draw upon forms such as ‘honeycombs, fingerprints, and patterns of insect movement.’ The first work that catches your eye is titled Apian Society, made with paper and gold foil texture paste. The artwork is in all shades of orange and bright yellow; in some ways, it also reminds me of the golden hour evenings. The artist says that this artwork explores collective living through a honeycomb structure, highlighting how individual contributions create a harmonious society without rivalry or envy. Another work that catches my attention is titled Constellation, made with acrylic on canvas; the work resembles a starry night, a rare occurance for city dwelling people. For the artist, it denotes the endless thoughts that inhabit a human mind. “From waking to sleeping, the flow of thoughts appearing and disappearing resembles a starry night sky, expressing the ceaseless flux and energy of countless thoughts,” says Ramki. For artist Ramesh, much of his works draw inspiration from his recent travels to Kochi in Kerala. He uses etching, woodcut, and mixed media to show crabs, boats, and the shore as recurring themes. In one work, dense tree roots envelop the boats, while in another, a school of fish swims alongside them. All these paintings seem to inherently carry forward a philosophy of mushrooming from one’s roots. How this expounds, measures their success. Internal voice The exhibition also brings to us many external philosophies. Born in Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, artist Surya S was raised in a village environment, which shaped his sensitivity to everyday life. His work General Perspective, made with a mixed media of paper, wood, and steel, resembles a pinball game with its metallic balls of varying sizes. But the artist says, “the things we witness, learn, accept, and question gradually shape our sense of identity and belonging. What begins as an external influence eventually becomes an internal voice.” Another artist who seems to contemplate the world as a whole is Murugesan. His works draw on scientific thought, philosophical enquiry, and close observations of Nature, ideas that are also echoed in their titles, such as Dialectics, Primary Energy, and Inter+Outer+Infinite. In Dialectics, made with graphite on paper, the artwork calls for multiple observations. Call it an optical illusion; the work seems to reveal itself differently every time, making it an object of intrigue. Yogeshwaran on the other hand, explores human emotion, resilience, strength, and the expressive possibilities of form. He transforms industrial materials like bronze, steel, and iron into forms that appear to float, rotate, or move through space. In one of his works, Midday Night, made with cotton steel, the sculpture captures a moment of celestial eclipse. “The spiralling, concentric metal bands represent the orbital motion of the cosmos, while the two polished central spheres embody the sun and moon becoming one,” he says. With Kannan’s steel work, Ramki Ravi’s paper work, Ramesh N’s woodcuts and etchings, Surya S’s mixed-media works, Mani Murugesan’s graphite explorations and Yogeshwaran V’s sculptures, the exhibition looks at material not merely as a medium, but as a carrier of memory, observation, and experience. Across these practices, materials are cut, layered, welded, etched and shaped, taking on meanings that extend beyond their physical qualities. Material Memoir is currently on Artiform, Mylapore till October 31. The sculptures are priced at ₹30,000 onwards. Published - October 03, 2026 06:57 pm IST

summary_clean: After the release of his debut album, Chennai-based musician Aryaman Singh, who goes by Sunflower Tape Machine is all set to perform at Music Matters in Singapore this October
body_clean: An artiste’s debut album is often their most personal piece of work — a distillation of the years, influences, instincts and experiments that led them to finding their voice. For Chennai-based independent musician Aryaman Singh, the new album is personal for another reason: it is five years of making music without ever quite setting out to make an album. “I didn’t start in 2021 thinking, ‘I’m going to make an album.’ All the songs I kept writing through the years just started making sense. At some point, I decided I wanted to stop releasing singles and put out an album. The narrative for my album at the time was: this is all the music I have, this is all the music I’ve made in the last few years, and I’m putting it in chronological order of it being made so you can see how I’ve evolved,” says Aryaman, who goes by Sunflower Tape Machine. Spanning eight tracks, I LIKE NOISE. MATTER OF FACT, I LOVE IT. is an indie/alternative rock record threaded with shoegaze (a subgenre of indie and alternative rock), with noise serving as its unifying force. The album moves between the more familiar Sunflower Tape Machine sound and a newer, more exploratory alt-rock territory, with a three-minute instrumental interlude of pure noise at its centre. “The order of tracks now on the album is what I think is the most cohesive order for you to experience the album. That being said, listen to the album in its entirety. It’s meant to be heard from start to finish,” says Aryaman. At around 25 minutes, it is a relatively compact listen. The album, however, was not always called I LIKE NOISE. MATTER OF FACT, I LOVE IT. When Aryaman first decided to turn his accumulated songs into an album, he had a different idea in mind: I Like Music, a chronological collection that would trace his evolution as a musician. That changed when he began listening back to the songs and noticed something tying them together. “I was sitting in the studio, and I was listening to a lot of the stuff that I was going to put on the album. I was like, ‘Wait. Eight of these songs have such a cohesive narrative.’ And that narrative was noise,” he says. For five years, Aryaman made the album largely on his own, writing, recording and mixing the songs at home. His creative process usually begins with an instrumental, followed by humming melodies and fitting words into them; the lyrics, he says, typically come last. “My music is very melody first. Usually it’s full instrumental and then I fit stuff into it, and usually it’s choruses first and then the verses come after,” he says. Like every other song he has made, the entire production happens in his room in Chennai. Even the drums on the album’s final two tracks were recorded there, with Nikhil Rajkumar, who plays live with Sunflower and with bands including Godless and Demonic Resurrection, coming in to play them. But Chennai has influenced more than just where the album was made. “I’ve grown up being a huge film guy, and a lot of the films that I’ve watched are the reason for my vocabulary today and just being up to date with pop culture. So, in that sense, Chennai and its access to other art forms and just everything has definitely influenced the art that I make,” says Aryaman. He also credits the city’s slower, close-knit way of life for shaping the experiences that eventually find their way into his music. The album’s five-year gestation also meant Aryaman had to reckon with an earlier version of himself. The first song he wrote for the record, I Saw You, dates back to 2021, and rather than rework it to fit his current sound, he deliberately left much of it untouched. “I made it a point not to change too much because I felt like it was 2021 Sunflower’s story, and I don’t want to take that away from him,” he says. The difference is audible: He describes it as innocent in its sound and selection. “You can kind of see that this was made by someone who really wanted to make this but didn’t have too much of an idea what he was doing.” Perhaps that is what makes I LIKE NOISE. MATTER OF FACT, I LOVE IT. feel less like a debut and more like a document of becoming. Aryaman has spent the last few years learning how to make music, learning the industry around it, and, in the process, learning how to recognise his own voice. He could have gone back and polished away the traces of the musician he was in 2021, but chose not to. Now, that five-year journey is taking him beyond Chennai. Aryaman will perform a set at Music Matters in Singapore, one of Asia’s leading music industry events. For an album that began as a collection of songs written without a larger plan, it feels like another step in Sunflower Tape Machine’s evolution — this time, taking the noise a little further from home. I LIKE NOISE. MATTER OF FACT, I LOVE IT. is now streaming on major music streaming platforms. Published - September 23, 2026 03:55 pm IST

The result was a culinary journey through the region. The welcome lunch featured a Kerala sadhya, followed by an Andhra-style high tea, a Karnataka-style breakfast, a traditional Tamil Nadu meal and for reception it was fusion menu comprising regional cuisines from across India and international cuisine. “Innovation and fusion in food have been trending over the past four or five years. Post-pandemic, people have become more willing to spend extravagantly on weddings, with couples and families investing in every aspect of the celebration,” says Sampath. For wedding caterers, such requests offer a glimpse into how the wedding feast is evolving — from a largely traditional spread to a more carefully curated experience, where regional cuisines, innovation, and personalisation increasingly find a place on the menu. All about customisation TP Rangaraj, popularly known as Madhampatty Rangaraj, who is at the helm of Madhampatty Thangavelu Hospitality, says that from a catering perspective, he has noticed a growing preference among couples for multi-cuisine menus and specific regional cuisines, including Chettinad, Kerala, and Andhra fare, alongside international menu offerings. His most popular dishes include the jackfruit biryani, guava chutney, and the sanguppo idiyappam-violet cabbage stew. “Families are willing to spend even ₹5,000 to ₹10,000 per head on a wedding meal. We have even flown down chefs from France, Italy, Japan, and Thailand to prepare authentic cuisine at weddings from these countries,” he says. Rangaraj also points to a shift in the scale of weddings. “Before the pandemic, families would invite 3,000 to 5,000 guests for a wedding. Over the past five years, the guest list has come down to around 1,000 to 2,000, but the focus is now on creating memorable moments for them, he says. Rangaraj adds that 24 years ago, when he entered the industry, it was the parents who decided the wedding menu, but these days, couples are actively involved in the process. “The trend now is towards concept-oriented menus, thematic buffet counters, and fusion and innovation in the food served,” he says. One reason for the growing demand for fusion menus and a mix of regional cuisines is the increasing number of inter-cultural marriages, says Siva Subramanian of Kamalambal Catering Services. With families from different culinary traditions coming together, wedding menus are increasingly becoming a way to represent and accommodate diverse food preferences. “Instagrammable weddings are trending. Whether it is the venue, with couples opting for beaches and outdoor settings, the decor or the food, there is a growing emphasis on innovation. Even the plating is given attention, because everything is shared on social media,” says Siva. He also points to a change in the nature of guest lists. “There are fewer guests, but greater spending and more elaborate food experiences per guest. Which is why, these days, no one wants to miss a wedding,” invitation,” he says. Social media, in particular, has given caterers a new brief: food has to taste good, but it also has to look good on camera. Resonating with these observations, MS Sriram of VCS Four Brothers Catering says, “dramatic and visually appealing live counters with catchy titles are a must. Dreamy dessert decks, with a range of ice creams, ‘Pulp at Your Point’ for fresh juices, street food counters, 90s-kids counters and Turkish ice cream are popular. A live dosa counter, where chutney is stone-ground and served fresh, is also popular.” Avant garde He adds that couples are willing to spend more on events such as the sangeet, mehendi, and haldi than on the wedding ceremony. He also notes a shift in who drives menu decisions. “Couples now interact directly with the caterers rather than leaving the decisions to their parents. In fact, couples are willing to spend more on events such as the sangeet, mehendi and haldi than they would on the ritualistic wedding ceremony,” says Sriram. While the buffet continues at some weddings, caterers say the format is also being rethought, with greater emphasis on live counters, table service, and smaller-batch cooking. Mamatha Caterers, for instance, offers dishes such as gongura spaghetti, adai pancakes, Madras ramen — coconut-milk rasam served with masala vada and sprinkled with vendakka crisps — and Marwadi khow suey. “For receptions, it is mostly a 50% fusion buffet menu, and we also offer personalised table service alongside the buffet,” says Sampath. “Buffets are no longer preferred at weddings, as this elimanates excessive food wastage,” says Sriram. of VCS Four Brothers Catering. Madhampatty Rangaraj attributes this partly to concerns over food wastage. “As caterers, we have to be careful about food wastage. Avoiding buffets helps eliminate wastage. Moreover, we cook in batches based on footfall,” he says, adding that he has now introduced tetrapack water bottles to avoid excessive plastic usage. With over a decade of experience in wedding planning, Ramkumar Varsham of Varsham Events says catering to Gen Z couples has made work easier, as they tend to have a clear vision of what they want and are mindful rather than lavish in their spending. Friends make up a larger share of the guest list rather than family, he adds. “While the couples spend around 30 to 40% per cent of the wedding expenses, the parents bear the rest. Young couples often prefer temple weddings with fewer than 100 guests and host the reception later, on a non-muhurtham date, when venues are more easily available. They also downsize the guest list but ensure that the guest experience is memorable, with When it comes to food during the muhurtam, however, tradition remains firmly in place,. “A traditional elai sappadu is never compromised for the muhurtham lunch. It is largely through social media that innovative and fusion menus are being showcased, and more events are being added prior to the wedding,” says Ramkumar. For all the experimentation taking place on the wedding menu, tradition has not disappeared from the plate. The muhurtham meal remains firmly rooted in regional culinary traditions, while receptions and other celebrations have become spaces for couples to experiment with personalised dining experiences. The shift, therefore, is not from traditional to modern, but towards a more curated celebration.For today’s couples, food is increasingly part of the entertainment and the experience — something to savour, remember and, inevitably, share. title: A hobby evolves to meet Gen Zers on their terms
title_clean: A hobby evolves to meet Gen Zers on their terms
title_normalized: a hobby evolves to meet gen zers on their terms
summary_clean: Advances in technology, easier licensing procedures and affordability are among the factors that make amateur radio attractive to youngsters, even those still in school. Here are perspectives of amateur radio enthusiasts and a seller of hobby-related equipment from Chennai
body_clean: There is usually an apocalyptic air to how Ham radio is perceived. The Ham radio enthusiast is readily visualised as trudging into a land overtaken by a massive disaster and where all technology-based communication lines outside the amateur-radio sphere have broken down. The enthusiast has morphed into a saviour, connecting with a fellow hobbyist elsewhere in the “universe” and communicating a local situation, dire and distressing, amidst the static and crackle of radio communication, to reach help to the suffering. This description is indeed fact-aligned. Ham radio enthusiasts do take centre stage during disasters. One witnessed that during the Kerala floods of 2018 and closer home, in the harrowing first week of December 2015 in Chennai. But distress communication is only one of the things riding on amateur radio airwaves. Net sessions (as on-air meetups of Ham radio hobbyists are known) are also defined by banter, in fact, more by small talk than SOS calls. And do not be surprised if the banter is punctuated with Gen Z lingo. N. Deepan (call sign VU2DPN), a key member of the Madras Amatuer Radio Society (MARS), points out that the Ham radio hobby has never been as accessible to youngsters as it is now. From licensing to practising the hobby, the procedures of initiation and the operation of the equipment have become ridiculously simple. Having seen 63 summers and getting started on the hobby around four decades ago, Deepan is at a vantage point to talk about the hobby’s evolution. The Wireless Planning and Coordination wing (WPC) is responsible for conducting Amateur Station Operator’s Certificate (ASOC) examinations and issuing the license. Deepan underlines the examinations have become simpler as technology has organically taken certain “subjects” off the table. And the removal of this barrier encourages the entry of youngsters. Anyone aged 12 and above can appear for the exam and get the license. “Where it took one or two years to get a license, it takes approximately one month,” observes Deepan, noting that objective questions have replaced the earlier pattern of examination. And the new license holder can hit the ground running, the process of getting started on the hobby also having become facile. EchoLink, Z3 DMR, and Droidstar allow licensed operators to communicate using just a phone with other amateur radio enthusiasts. Once the license is validated, usually within 24 hours, the software can be used. And that obviates the need to invest in ham radio equipment; that can wait. Deepan has seen the ham radio equipment move from valves to transistors, ICs and now Software Defined Radio (SDR). With advancing technology, the equipment has shrunk, and so has their prices. Deepan attributes the fall in prices to the shift from imported equipment to local dealerships (to sell ham radio equipment, a dealer’s license is required). That brings us to someone like Gaurav Srivatsava and his wife Shivangi Gaurav, both ham radio license holders and diehard enthusiasts, and beyond that, owners of Radio Brewery in Iyyapanthangal (radiobrewery.com), which sells amatuer radio equipment. Shivangi largely manages the business while Gaurav continues to work in the IT sector. Their own personal struggles in finding reliable and cost-effective equipment locally had crystallised into this business venture in 2018. Gaurav recalls that besides importing, Ham radio enthusiasts in Chennai were dependent on a couple of dealers in Delhi. The hobbyists would together buy in bulk to keep prices within their comfort range. Among those who encouraged them to start this business was Deepan, one of Gaurav’s mentors and supporters. Among factors that augur well for the hobby, Gaurav says, is the portability of the ham radio gear. He recalls the time when valve radios, measuring six by six feet, “appropriated” a room in exchange for the joy of communicating on amateur radio airwaves. Fast forward to now, low-powered ham radio equipment can “fit into a small bread box”. Deepan notes that even if one were to route their ham radio communication through an amateur radio satellite, the allied equipment, which includes SDR dongle, dish antenna and up converter or transverter, is easy on the back, being eminently portable. Both Deepan and Gaurav have noticed youngsters taking to the hobby. Gaurav points out his daughter Pari Gaurav (VI2JXB/ KN6GRI, US amateur radio identifier ID), 19 years old now, cleared the WPC examination at age 12. Deepan’s daughter, Malini D. (VU3JJT) is also an avid ham radio enthusiast. Even youngsters without any precedent of ham radio engagement in their families are gravitating towards the hobby for the doors of communication it opens in various parts of the world. Deepan notes, “On the Net, all radio ham hobbyists connect and converse as equals.” To sum up, this hobby seems to have been made for Gen Zers (and the ones following them too) for two reasons. It is a generation that derives its strength and purpose from communication, even with those they will never meet in real life, and this hobby is geared to that. And two, this generation thrives on volunteering, and this hobby can provide opportunities for that during extremely harrowing times. ( Niche Trades & Hobbiesis a column that tracks businesses that deal in rare products and follows groups that need those products to keep their hobbies going) Published - October 04, 2026 08:50 am IST

Net sessions (as on-air meetups of Ham radio hobbyists are known) are also defined by banter, in fact, more by small talk than SOS calls. And do not be surprised if the banter is punctuated with Gen Z lingo. N. Deepan (call sign VU2DPN), a key member of the Madras Amatuer Radio Society (MARS), points out that the Ham radio hobby has never been as accessible to youngsters as it is now. From licensing to practising the hobby, the procedures of initiation and the operation of the equipment have become ridiculously simple. Having seen 63 summers and getting started on the hobby around four decades ago, Deepan is at a vantage point to talk about the hobby’s evolution. The Wireless Planning and Coordination wing (WPC) is responsible for conducting Amateur Station Operator’s Certificate (ASOC) examinations and issuing the license. Deepan underlines the examinations have become simpler as technology has organically taken certain “subjects” off the table. And the removal of this barrier encourages the entry of youngsters. Anyone aged 12 and above can appear for the exam and get the license. “Where it took one or two years to get a license, it takes approximately one month,” observes Deepan, noting that objective questions have replaced the earlier pattern of examination. And the new license holder can hit the ground running, the process of getting started on the hobby also having become facile. EchoLink, Z3 DMR, and Droidstar allow licensed operators to communicate using just a phone with other amateur radio enthusiasts. Once the license is validated, usually within 24 hours, the software can be used. And that obviates the need to invest in ham radio equipment; that can wait. Deepan has seen the ham radio equipment move from valves to transistors, ICs and now Software Defined Radio (SDR). With advancing technology, the equipment has shrunk, and so has their prices. Deepan attributes the fall in prices to the shift from imported equipment to local dealerships (to sell ham radio equipment, a dealer’s license is required). That brings us to someone like Gaurav Srivatsava and his wife Shivangi Gaurav, both ham radio license holders and diehard enthusiasts, and beyond that, owners of Radio Brewery in Iyyapanthangal (radiobrewery.com), which sells amatuer radio equipment. Shivangi largely manages the business while Gaurav continues to work in the IT sector. Their own personal struggles in finding reliable and cost-effective equipment locally had crystallised into this business venture in 2018. Gaurav recalls that besides importing, Ham radio enthusiasts in Chennai were dependent on a couple of dealers in Delhi. The hobbyists would together buy in bulk to keep prices within their comfort range. Among those who encouraged them to start this business was Deepan, one of Gaurav’s mentors and supporters. Among factors that augur well for the hobby, Gaurav says, is the portability of the ham radio gear. He recalls the time when valve radios, measuring six by six feet, “appropriated” a room in exchange for the joy of communicating on amateur radio airwaves. Fast forward to now, low-powered ham radio equipment can “fit into a small bread box”. Deepan notes that even if one were to route their ham radio communication through an amateur radio satellite, the allied equipment, which includes SDR dongle, dish antenna and up converter or transverter, is easy on the back, being eminently portable. Both Deepan and Gaurav have noticed youngsters taking to the hobby. Gaurav points out his daughter Pari Gaurav (VI2JXB/ KN6GRI, US amateur radio identifier ID), 19 years old now, cleared the WPC examination at age 12. Deepan’s daughter, Malini D. (VU3JJT) is also an avid ham radio enthusiast. Even youngsters without any precedent of ham radio engagement in their families are gravitating towards the hobby for the doors of communication it opens in various parts of the world. Deepan notes, “On the Net, all radio ham hobbyists connect and converse as equals.” To sum up, this hobby seems to have been made for Gen Zers (and the ones following them too) for two reasons. It is a generation that derives its strength and purpose from communication, even with those they will never meet in real life, and this hobby is geared to that. And two, this generation thrives on volunteering, and this hobby can provide opportunities for that during extremely harrowing times. title_en: A hobby evolves to meet Gen Zers on their terms

Here are the details of 71-year-old Seshadri’s second innings: a Press Information Bureau-accredited international sports photographer from Chennai and a Canon EOS Ambassador. He now has a reputation for “checking into” major international sporting events. As this article is being written, he is shooting images of sporting excellence at the 20th Asian Games, unfolding at Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya in Japan. Before zooming in on what he is doing now, a quick run of his first innings: Sukumar had been working in the banking sector, being an official photographer with Indian Overseas Bank (IOB). He always had an intense desire to be a sports photographer, but that remained a desire for a drearily long time. When retirement from his corporate career was looming large, Sukumar took the plunge and started pursuing sports photography full steam ahead. After Sukumar had been years into sports photography, in 2021, Sukumar’s nephew shared a story about his uncle’s passion for sports photography online. Sukumar was 66 years old then and covering the Tokyo Olympic Games. And the story of how someone is flourishing in a career kickstarted mid-life caught the world’s imagination. Sukuamar’s portfolio includes multiple Olympic Games, FIFA World Cups (including the most recent edition), ICC World Cups, Grand Slam tournaments, Asian Games, Commonwealth Games, NBA events, FINA World Championships, FIDE World Cups and MotoGP, among several other major sporting events. Among his iconic photographs is one of the Rio Olympics, one that captured the contrasting emotions of the winner and the loser; the photograph won him a gold medal from the Photographic Society of America (PSA). Sukumar’s professional photographs have been distributed through international wire services and stock photography libraries, including Alamy, Zuma Press, IMAGO Images, SOPA Images and Reuters Connect. Sukumar’s life and career are a reminder that it is never too late to start afresh. Published - October 04, 2026 09:52 am IST

body_clean: MGM Healthcare Malar, Adyar, has introduced ultra-low-dose CT chest screening and low-dose CT coronary angiography, using deep-learning AI technology and quantitative imaging, to enable earlier and more precise detection of cancer and coronary artery disease. At a press meet on Tuesday (September 22, 2026), doctors said the approach substantially reduces radiation exposure while preserving the lung architecture needed for diagnosis. Thinesh Ram, senior consultant radiologist, said invasive imaging through cardiac catheterisation remains a mainstay for assessing coronary artery disease, while non-invasive techniques such as multidetector CT (MDCT) offer a quicker and relatively affordable alternative. The approach is aimed at reducing both radiation and contrast exposure while maintaining the image quality required to assess the coronary arteries. A key component of the low-dose coronary CT and ultra-low-dose chest CT workflow is Delta, a deep-learning-based image reconstruction technology that enables diagnostically useful images to be reconstructed from scans acquired at substantially lower radiation doses and, in selected applications, lower volumes of contrast, said Dr. Reefath. Ms. Eden said road accidents had declined compared with last year, mainly due to awareness programmes led by the police, greater public awareness, greater compliance with helmet rules among two-wheeler riders, strict enforcement, and fines issued based on automatic number plate recognition camera footage. She said the ongoing Metro Rail and flyover works led to traffic congestion, particularly on Anna Salai in Saidapet and Teynampet. Traffic movement is expected to improve significantly, once these works are completed. “We are taking measures to ease traffic congestion on the OMR and ECR by deploying additional personnel at key points and regulating traffic flow,” she said. summary_clean: The Northeast monsoon is at Chennai’s doorstep. This year, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has predicted normal Northeast monsoon rainfall, with a strong El Niño likely to strengthen it further towards the end of the year. Historically, November and December have, for long, been months to remember in the city, where rains can be unpredictable. With the monsoon getting shorter and more intense over the past few years, successive Dravidian governments had grappled with mitigation measures, only to be overwhelmed time and again by the ferocity of nature. Is the new Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government prepared to face the monsoon, or will Chennai have to brace for another deluge? R. Aishwaryaa takes a deeper look.
body_clean: Call it the continuum or an early image-building exercise, Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, who also holds the Municipal Administration portfolio, has already deployed Ministers and senior officials to take up flood-mitigation works well ahead of the onset of the Northeast monsoon. He has instructed that all de-silting and stormwater drain (SWD) works be completed as early as possible. Official data shows that the flood-vulnerable locations within the Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) have dropped from nearly 800 in 2015 to 389 in 2023. The figure is 219 for the 2026 Northeast monsoon. The list of vulnerable locations is being continuously reviewed based on field-level assessments, rainfall patterns, and the effectiveness of the completed flood-mitigation works, said GCC officials. The micro-level SWD works are 95% complete, but there are severe capacity constraints along the Buckingham Canal, Adyar, and Sholinganallur, officials added. GCC Commissioner G.S Sameeran said the civic body is coordinating with the Railways, Chennai Metro Rail Limited, and other agencies on drainage and flood-mitigation works. “Some major infrastructure works may take longer. The GCC has implemented temporary solutions, such as pumping facilities, for managing the monsoon,” he said. Lack of consultation Mr. Sameeran and his team have been on routine inspections – almost daily – of various works across the city. Even so, there has been talk about a lack of consultation and transparency in the conduct of flood-mitigation works. MDMK councillor S. Jeevan of Ward 35 in Perambur said, “Elected representatives do not know what is happening during flood preparedness inspections. I have not been able to meet the assistant engineer for 10 days to discuss residents’ complaints. The flood risk is high this year due to delays in desilting canals such as the Kodungaiyur Canal.” Federation of North Chennai Residents Welfare Association president T. Shanmugam said residents were worried as officials had not shared details of flood preparedness yet. Haris Sulthan, an activist in Padi, said most waterbodies in and around Chennai and its suburbs remained largely dry, with the five drinking water reservoirs together holding 4.5 TMC against the 11.7 TMC total capacity. He said routine annual works were being carried out, but no new major flood-mitigation interventions had been undertaken beyond these works in many areas, including Medavakkam, Chitlapakkam, Hasthinapuram, Kadaperi, Ambedkar Road, Jothi Nagar, and Sunnambu Kolathur, where prolonged inundation was reported previously. He appreciated the cancellation/reversal of tenders of “cosmetical lake-front development” works by the newly elected TVK government, while also calling for further desilting, the removal of water hyacinth, and increasing the lake depth. Urbanisation challenge According to a senior official in the GCC, Chennai’s monsoon vulnerability, particularly in the south of the city, is largely due to unchecked urbanisation, and that flooding in many parts like near Perumbakkam is “100% man-made”. Pointing to the built-up spaces and encroachments around the Pallikaranai marshland, Perungudi, and the IT corridor, he said that natural watercourses are choked, and canals in T. Nagar and Mambalam are heavily polluted because the “entire waterway is a sewer due to illegal sewage connections.” K.P. Subramanian, an urban planner, highlighted that while flood resilience in Velachery has improved, areas like Kuber Nagar, Karthikeyapuram, and parts of Madipakkam still face risks due to urban development and drain silting. He recommends regular desilting and zoning regulations to designate flood plains, river, and lake margins as no-development zones. D. Raghunandan, a climate researcher at Delhi Science Forum, said the SWD network in Chennai and its suburbs must be redesigned to handle extreme rainfall events such as 100-200 mm or more in just a few hours, rather than just evenly distributed volumes of rain. Instead of a haphazard pattern of urbanisation, the buildings, roads, and flyovers must be planned to ensure natural drainage and that the connectivity of stormwater drains to the three major rivers running through the city, and eventually into the sea, is not affected. Chennai must protect its wetlands and lakes such as in Perumbakkam, Pallikaranai; the depth of the Cooum and Adyar rivers have also reduced compared to yesteryears. Increasing the capacity of waterbodies would help store excess rainfall water or drain it naturally towards the sea, he suggested. “These are long and costly overhaul processes that have to be addressed systematically over time, but they would pay back by offsetting losses during frequent urban floods,” he noted, adding that similar measures were needed in all major cities, not just in Chennai. S. Janakarajan, president of the South Asia Consortium for Interdisciplinary Water Resources Studies and former professor at MIDS, said water conservation must be prioritised since short, heavy downpours are the new normal. He said 70% to 80% of rainfall runs off into the sea because departments uncoordinatedly drain water, and suggested that the State focus on conservation to mitigate floods and droughts. “There are 4,100 lakes in the three adjoining districts [Tiruvallur, Chengalpattu, and Kancheepuram], besides numerous temple tanks and ponds that can help augment surface water and improve groundwater recharge. Also, temporary holding ponds could be created in educational institutions, parks, playfields, and government land, while large private land parcels could also be considered for creating sponge parks,” he said. Monsoon preparedness The WRD, meanwhile, is set to complete the first phase of its annual desilting exercise in a week. However, vast swathes of water hyacinth hindering the free flow of floodwater in waterways remain a challenge this year, too. While the department has accelerated work to clean the major and minor waterways ahead of the Northeast monsoon, residents of various parts of the city have urged the authorities to coordinate with other agencies to prevent sewage from entering the waterways. The department has deployed about 400 machines, including floating excavators, to clean the waterways, including Adyar, Cooum, Kosasthalaiyar, and Araniyar rivers, as well as the Buckingham canal, and also clear sand bars at the various river mouths. Officials noted that the ₹42-crore project would help minimise flooding in the rivers and backflow into micro drains by 70% to 80% during the monsoon. The rivers would be able to handle the flows without spillover, even in the event of 200 mm of rainfall in a day. Sewer networks To reduce sewage-related complaints during the ensuing Northeast monsoon, Chennai Metrowater has completed the second phase of cleaning the city’s sewer network. The network was cleaned through 41,996 manholes during this phase, carried out between July and September. As floodwater often enters the sewer network during heavy rain, the water agency plans to undertake a third phase of cleaning between October and December to minimise blockages and prevent sewer network failures, officials said. Nearly 417 sewage pumping stations and sewage treatment plants have been equipped with IoT-based monitoring systems to help detect and prevent sewage stagnation and overflows. Robotic equipment is also being used to detect leaks and damages in drinking water pipelines. Power infrastructure The Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) covers flood mitigation works under 22 categories. The monsoon preparatory works are carried out on a massive scale this year, a senior official of the TNPDCL said. Tree branch clearance was completed at 6.75 lakh locations, exposed underground cables were buried at 1,762 places, damaged insulators were replaced at 85,000 locations, and low-sag overhead lines were rectified at 54,387 places. Maintenance is under way at 2,650 substations and 3,840 pillar boxes. The TNPDCL is also replacing 40,000 damaged concrete poles and worn-out conductors at 2,500 locations. Distribution transformer structures are maintained at 60,000 places, according to data shared by the TNPDCL. Maintenance works are nearly complete across distribution regions, barring Chennai North, Central, West, and South-I. Over 90% of monsoon preparatory works are done in Chennai South-II, Kancheepuram, and Tiruvallur, data showed. Works are expedited in central Chennai (T. Nagar, Anna Salai, Teynampet, Royapettah, Triplicane, and Mylapore), where only 52% of the works have been completed. In the western region covering Ambattur, Avadi, Maduravoyal, Anna Nagar, and Kolathur, 56% of the works are complete. ‘Early preparedness is key’ “Local bodies across Tamil Nadu have been directed to complete monsoon works by October 10. In Chennai, desilting has been under way for two and a half months, with one cycle covering nearly one lakh silt catch pits having been completed. The second cycle is under way. Similar instructions have been issued to other corporations, municipalities, and town panchayats,” said Municipal Administration and Water Supply (MAWS) Department Secretary Gagandeep Singh Bedi. “Very high rainfall in short duration and rainwater inflow from adjoining suburban areas would place more pressure on the SWD systems, so early preparedness is key,” he told the department heads at a recent meeting. summary_clean: The initiative by the school is built around the theme “75 Years, 75,000 Trees, One Living Legacy”
body_clean: Staff and students of Chinmaya Vidyalaya at Taylor’s Road in Kilpauk have begun to put their green thumbs to work. Recently, the school launched “Chinmaya Amritavanam”, an ambitious initiative to plant and nurture 75,000 trees to commemorate 75 years of the Chinmaya Mission, during the school’s 59th Annual Day celebrations. This would mean every activity around planting and nurturing these saplings will involve students across classes. Built around the theme “75 Years, 75,000 Trees, One Living Legacy,” the initiative envisages planting 1,000 trees for every year of Chinmaya Mission’s journey, creating a lasting green legacy while engaging students and the wider community in environmental stewardship, says a press note. The school has chalked out a plan to fulfil this mission of increasing the green cover in and around the city. Geetha Ganesh, principal, Chinmaya Vidyalaya, says the school will be responsible for taking care of the plants for the next five years, and they are implementing the project in a phased manner involving other institutions as well. “There are eight other sister schools of Chinmaya Vidyalaya in the city who will also be part of this initiative, they will be taking saplings and growing them on their campus. Likewise, our neighbouring schools Bhavan’s Rajaji Vidyasharm and Maharishi Vidya Mandir in Chetpet have also agreed to be part of the green drive,” says Geetha. The plants are geo-tagged, which means the GPS coordinates and species details will be available. Among activities that the school is planning include a visit to Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited where students would initiate the drive. The event Chinmaya Amritavanam was formally inaugurated by V. Karunapriya, Additional Principal Chief Conservator of Forests and Managing Director, TAFCORN. Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) will receive 5,000 saplings for Green Belt Development at Amullavoyal, Manali. Sri Sriram Vishwanathan, Chief General Manager (HSE), CPCL, received a sapling on behalf of CPCL, marking the first major commitment towards the 75,000-tree goal. The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) is also partnering with Chinmaya Vidyalaya in taking the initiative forward. B. Chandra Mohan, IAS; Leena Nair, IAS (Retd.), Chairperson, Chinmaya Vidyalayas, Chennai; O. V. Nambiar, Zonal Director, Chinmaya Vidyalayas, Chennai; Sri Jaishankar Unnithan, Honorary Correspondent were among the special guests at the event. Published - September 26, 2026 10:49 pm IST

body_clean: Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) councillors sought to expand the scope of works covered under the first phase of the Ward Development Fund, at the council meeting on Friday. Standing Committee Chairperson C. Velu said the councillors were asked to use the ₹30 lakh allocated for pre-monsoon works such as improving roads, cleaning storm-water drains, purchasing boats, building retaining walls, and installing CCTV cameras. He asked whether the allocation was additional or would be drawn from the existing funds. If the councillors were restricted to using the fund only for the works listed, they would be unable to attend to other maintenance requirements, he said. GCC Commissioner G.S. Sameeran said pre-monsoon works were given priority, and that councillors could identify locations that require immediate attention. Thiru.Vi.Ka Nagar councillor Siva. Raajashekaran said they were unable to undertake even minor works such as welding because of the restrictions on the funds. Deputy Mayor M. Magesh Kumaar and many councillors demanded that a revised circular be issued on the usage of funds. Standing Committee (Revenue) Chairperson Sarbajaya Das said zonal officials had told councillors that the funds could be used only for monsoon-related works, and sought a circular clarifying the position. Mr. Sameeran said the funds could be used for works other than monsoon preparedness and agreed to issue a circular to this effect. Remarks draw flak Valasaravakkam Ward Committee Chairperson V. Rajan criticised certain remarks allegedly made by Minister for Public Works Department (PWD) Aadhav Arjuna in the Assembly during the recent Budget session on the functioning of elected representatives and DMK mayors in municipal corporations. Mr. Rajan said councillors and committee chairpersons were not receiving adequate funds and were not being invited to meetings held by Ministers at Ripon Buildings or to inaugurations across the city. Mayor R. Priya asked Mr. Rajan to “become an MLA and pose this question in the Assembly”. DMK floor leader R. Ramalingam said the Minister should explain his remarks at a council meeting. The Mayor said she could grant permission for this. T. Nagar BJP councillor Uma Anandan said officials of the Electricity Board, Metrowater, and the GCC did not cooperate with the councillors, and that the role of councillors was becoming redundant. Valasaravakkam councillor S. Bharathi sought clarity on the monitoring of storm-water drain connections. Referring to the ongoing work to lay new drains on Arcot Road, she asked whether the underground high-tension cables were being properly shifted or whether drains were being laid over them. The Mayor said the work had been awarded to Narayana Constructions and that the underground cables were being shifted during excavations. Damaged or severed cables, if any, were being replaced before the work proceeded, she said. Ms. Bharathi, however, alleged that she had submitted photographs showing lack of progress, and called for an inspection. Mr. Sameeran said the pictures had been taken during construction and that the location had since been revamped, and the high-tension cables relocated. Four contracts awarded Tondiarpet Ward Committee chairperson Nethaji U. Ganesan said four contracts had been awarded in the past four months, including works for desilting drains and repairing damaged roads, at 34% and 36% below the estimated amounts. Mr. Ganesan questioned the quality of such works and alleged that officials were not monitoring them regularly. He added that motor repair works were being delayed. The Mayor asked the Commissioner to examine whether a cap — with a limit of around 15% — could be fixed on bids below the estimated cost, depending on the nature of the work. body_clean: What does a day in the life of a 13-year-old who dreams of representing India in football look like? For S Hariharan, it means waking up at 4am, and juggling school with two training sessions. All this six days a week. The long days can be demanding, but this football player casually calls it a small sacrifice to achieve a bigger dream. “I started playing football at the age of 10 and never turned back. I saw my dad playing and wanted to try it. He was my first coach,” says Hariharan. Although it initially started as a fun game, Hariharan was intrigued by the benefits and opportunities that sports brought to an individual. “There are many Government employees living near my home who got jobs through the sports quota playing football. This made me want to play the sport seriously,” he says. Thus, his journey began at the Netaji Football Club in Vyasarpadi in North Chennai. Known as a mini-Brazil, there is no dearth of football players in the locality. “Everyone in my neighbourhood likes football. You will find a football player in every family here,” says Hariharan. Hariharan was able to kickstart his journey through Chennai Kaalpandu League(CKL) season 4, a grassroots football initiative organised by LatentView Analytics, for children from Government schools who cannot afford and lack access to structured sports coaching. “Leagues like CKL give us free jerseys, boots, and practice sessions. That’s what motivated me to participate in CKL initially,” he says. CKL became instrumental in his selection for the Sports Authority of India (SAI) boarding training programme at Don Bosco Matriculation School, Perambur. His performance in CKL also landed him a place in the Chennaiyin FC. For Hariharan, each of these opportunities became a stage to improve his skills and physical fitness. “Children from my locality come up to me and say they want to play football after looking at me,” he says, adding that his sister, Hasini Shree also plays in the CKL . For all the bigger fields he has played in, his most cherished memory remains the local tournament in Vyasarpadi where his team fought back from a draw and eventually won in a tie-breaker, as his parents, teachers and friends cheered him on. “Whenever I have a tournament, my parents, neighbours, and friends come to cheer. Although I feel very nervous to play while they watch the match from the gallery, once the match is over, I am simply happy that they came to cheer me up,” he adds. As a fan of Argentine footballer Emiliano Martínez, Hariharan says he admires the goalkeeper’s techniques. He also spends time watching UEFA Champions League videos on YouTube, picking up new techniques and trying them out on the field. He says learning on his own has helped him improve his game. While success brings him happiness, Hariharan says he has also learnt to look at failure as an opportunity to do better in the next match. “My coach, Illavarasan, and Jaya Singh help me cope with failure. They ask me to look forward and win the next game. That motivates me,” he says. Although he calls football his life, he also dreams of becoming an IAS officer. Through this dream, he hopes to bring about a lot of change in Vyasarpadi. “I hope to provide free football classes for children in Vyasarpadi, and also provide them with sports equipments, jerseys, and nutrition.” Published - September 22, 2026 11:32 am IST

summary_clean: From handrails in an apartment complex to a pool lift, here are some examples of how a little initiative can transform everyday living for senior citizens and those with special needs
body_clean: How accessible is your apartment community? That’s the central idea of this short film Block A For Accessibility, released with a private screening at PVR Satyam Cinemas on September 25. The 20-minute CBFC-certified film by YWTC (Yes, We Too Can!!!) Charitable Trust, in collaboration with Fiserv and United Way Mumbai as the CSR partner, is a story of care, community, and design. The film revolves around Natarajan, an ageing father, who after starting to use a wheelchair keeps himself isolated from the vibrant life of his apartment complex because he does not want to trouble his son. A sudden accident at the building’s stairs becomes a turning point for the entire community. The film follows the internal realisation of the association secretary and the decisive action of the builder. Natarajan’s character is played by a deaf person, Ravi Kumar. Voice was given by Umapathy, a wheelchair user. Most of the cast and crew are persons with disabilities, including the director. The film has sign language interpretations along with subtitles. The film addresses a universal civic necessity: accessible housing that accommodates an ageing population and ensures people of all abilities live with independence and dignity. For a screening of “Block A For Accessibility” at your apartment complex/workplace, write to yeswetoocan@gmail.com Handrails: a silver jubilee gift Not many residents at Raheja Regency, a 25-year-old apartment community in MRC Nagar, likely know the two people who were instrumental in getting handrails installed at strategic points in the society recently. Nonagenarian Arjun Krishna and Vasantha Arjun were too modest to talk about this accessibility feature and agreed to give their names after much prodding by this journalist. One of the earliest residents of this gated community, when the couple were part of the resident association, they got handrails fixed at most of the blocks some 20 years ago. These have been patronised by all, especially the senior citizens. But the community could do with some more, and the couple themselves have experienced the practical difficulty in not having them. “One of the ladies has even fallen not having a railing to hold on to it,” says Vasantha. The couple sponsored the entire cost of installing the handrailings at some new locations as a gift to the community that has been their home for the last 25 years (the couple marked 25 years of staying in the community this June). Pool lift: for easy swimming Madhavi Latha Prathigudupu’s day is not complete without accessing the swimming pool at her gated community in Arumbakkam. Since 2022, what makes this common amenity accessible for this para-athlete is the pool lift that was incorporated. The swimming champion cannot do without being in the pool and her late father had to help her get into the waters. She convinced Triumph Apartments, a community with 108 flats where she owns one, to make the pool accessible. “Before installing the pool lift, we had a demonstration done by the manufacturer with the committee members to get their approval,” says Madhavi, president of YWTC Charitable Trust. Today, she goes independently into the pool (she controls the lift pool through a remote) and most importantly has raised the importance of having inclusive amenities at gated communities not just for those with disabilities but even for use by the elderly. There was no ramp when she moved in to the community; the association did not just construct one for access to her block but made the improvisation at other towers as well. Accessibility standards of the National Building Code insist on a barrier-free built environment and all common facilities accessible to all people. “It’s your right, so ask the builder for such accessible features before investing in a flat,” she adds. Sensory park: designed by special parents In August, the Community Living Association for Parents of Special Citizens (CLAPS) celebrated four years of moving into an inclusively designed campus at Tiruvallur, near Poondi reservoir. A group of 50 parents of young adults with special needs got together to conceptualise such a model in a 8.5 acre residential campus that comes with a host of universally designed and accessible amenities. Latha Krishnan and Vaijayanthi Srinivasan, both special parents, say the activity centre, swimming pool, and sensory park are the most popular among the young adults aged 20 and above. Unlike the apartment communities where they faced many challenges, here everything is customised in keeping with the different needs of the children, a majority are on the spectrum, some with Down’s Syndrome and intellectually disability. The sensory park, for instance, is a hit for those with autism and has equipment with different textures. The activity centre allows them choose programmes as per one’s moods and likes. To oversee the children, there are many external professionals, including the warden, supervisor and activity head. Published - October 03, 2026 10:10 pm IST

Viji of Srinivasapuram, the other leader bringing people together, said that fishermen had been demanding that around ten thousand slum clearance board tenements should be demolished and reconstructed. Some of these buildings were constructed during former Chief Minister K. Kamaraj’s time and also in the 1970s. There has been no maintenance after the tsunami of 2004. We also want the government to construct homes for non-fishermen who live amongst us in these villages,” he demanded. Published - September 30, 2026 05:30 am IST

title: India’s growing elderly population needs an integrated care system, says report
title_clean: India’s growing elderly population needs an integrated care system, says report
title_normalized: india s growing elderly population needs an integrated care system says report
summary_clean: The report calls for better integration of wellness and chronic care, home care, assisted living, rehabilitation, memory care and palliative and end-of-life care
body_clean: India’s ageing population will require senior living to be accompanied by accessible care services, including assisted living, rehabilitation, memory care and home-based care, according to a report released by the Association of Senior Living India (ASLI) on Monday. The report, Silver Surge 2.0 – From Places to Care: Building India’s Senior Care Continuum, estimates that India’s population aged 60 and above will reach 166.9 million in 2026 and about 347 million by 2050. It notes that organised senior living penetration remains at about 1.5%, while assisted living accounts for less than 10% of organised senior living stock. The report also estimates that about 8.8 million Indians are living with dementia and 12.2% of seniors have supportive or palliative care needs. It identifies workforce capacity, financing and quality standards as key gaps. Initially, the Avadi police registered a case of suspicious death, as there were no obvious signs of assault, and sent the body to the Government Kilpauk Medical College Hospital for a post mortem. An argument broke out between them, following which Madan allegedly forced sand into Vasanthakumar’s mouth and left the place. Police suspect Vasanthakumar, who was heavily intoxicated, suffocated after the sand blocked his airway and died on the spot. The police subsequently altered the case to murder and arrested Madan on Friday. He was produced before a court and remanded in judicial custody at Puzhal Central Prison. body_clean: A change in mindset is needed for corporate social responsibility (CSR) to create a meaningful impact, rather than merely meet compliance requirements, speakers said at a session at The Hindu Sustainability Summit 2026 in Chennai on Wednesday (September 23, 2026). Addressing the session, titled Responsibility to Impact: Driving sustainable CSR through ESG, Data and Digital Innovation, Rohit Kumar Agrawala, Director (Finance), CPCL, said the environmental, social and governance (ESG) framework has become integral to the ecosystem driving industrial growth and is no longer merely a compliance requirement. Critical resources cannot be ignored in business management and decision-making, said Mr. Agrawala, who sought to highlight how refinery operations can no longer be viewed in isolation, as the cost of production, competitiveness and CSR are interconnected. Pointing out that sustainability targets in CPCL are more focused on implementation than intent, he said peer collaboration is also important to scale sustainable solutions and create changes in society. “We need to move beyond incremental changes and shift from linear to exponential growth in our sustainability efforts,” Mr. Agrawala said and added that CSR metrics should focus not on money spent but on measurable outcomes and impact. Speakers observed that CSR has evolved from merely counting beneficiaries to understanding their needs and measuring the impact of interventions, driven in part by regulatory requirements. Geetha Ramamoorthi, founder and principal advisor, Herizon Advisory, said health and education account for a significant share of CSR interventions among the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Other SDGs, including sustainable industries and communities, must be brought to the centre of CSR efforts, she said. A green innovation fund should be created to help startups develop innovative solutions, while cross-skilling programmes can help micro, small and medium industries (MSMEs) build the capabilities needed for the green transition, said Ms. Ramamoorthi. She also called for greater awareness of sustainability among the future workforce through the introduction of project-based learning in educational institutions. Creating a wider impact in society requires a shift in mindset along with sustained commitment and collective action, she said. Noting that ESG data largely remains in the reporting phase, Akshay Kurian, head of consulting and supply chain sustainability at Treeni Sustainability Solutions, said it plays an important role in setting a baseline and tracking progress. With many companies focusing on renewable energy and reducing emissions, Mr. Kurian said ESG data plays a crucial role in decision-making by helping organisations assess progress made and identify areas for improvement. For instance, tracking attrition levels provides insights into workforce trends. Pointing out that the capability of MSMEs is faster than that of larger companies in addressing sustainability, he said a mindset shift is important to build their capacity for the green transition. The session was moderated by Geetha Srimathi, senior reporter, The Hindu. The summit is supported by Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) as the Presenting Partner, with NLC India Limited, Larsen & Toubro (L&T), Navin’s, WABAG, Tamil Nadu Newsprint and Papers Limited, Indian Bank, Urbando and State Bank of India as Associate Partners. The summit’s sustainability-focused partnerships include Thermax as the Sustainable Cooling Partner, Treeni as the Sustainability Intelligence Partner, Chennai Port Authority as the Blue Economy Partner and Tamil Nadu Green Climate Company as the Climate Action Partner. summary_clean: Judge Colony and Neighbourhood Welfare Association raises concerns over drainage, groundwater contamination and road safety
body_clean: The newly formed Judge Colony and Neighbourhood Welfare Association, an initiative of the United Federation of Residents Welfare Associations in Tambaram City Corporation, has raised concerns over high property tax rates, groundwater contamination, inadequate drainage, poor roads and road safety. The association was formally inaugurated on September 27 in the presence of more than 100 residents. It has also submitted a memorandum to the Chief Minister’s Special Cell and the Municipal Administration and Water Supply Department (MAWS) seeking action on the issues. Property tax burden One of the major issues raised by the association was the property tax rates in Tambaram Corporation. S.M. Govindarajan, social activist, said the property tax revised by the Corporation in 2024 was significantly higher than that in several premium localities in Greater Chennai. According to Govindarajan, the property tax for a 1,500 sq ft residential building in Zone A of Tambaram Corporation was ₹26,812.65, which he said was 65% higher than the tax for a comparable property on Boat Club Road and 164% higher than that on North Usman Road, despite the latter having a lower guideline value. He said Chitlapakkam residents were facing a disproportionately high property tax burden despite relatively lower guideline values. He also said that, as per local body norms, an Appeals Committee comprising the Mayor/Commissioner and councillors, irrespective of political affiliation, should be in place. “There is no information on this and there was no public consultation or discussion among councillors before revising the tax rates,” he said. “Despite writing to Tambaram Corporation on this issue, zero action has been taken to date. Residents are forced to face a second property tax hike of 178%–550%, well above the 25%–100% ceiling fixed by the MAWS in G.O. 52 of March 2022,” he said. The association said it hoped for a positive response to its memorandum. Till then, it urged the Corporation to refrain from fixing a deadline for payment of the revised property tax. Civic and safety concerns Residents of Sriram Colony expressed concern over possible groundwater contamination by septic water and persistent drainage problems. According to Govindarajan, streets in Sriram Colony, in Ward 34, Zone 3, Tambaram Sanatorium, were flooded even during gentle downpours. As the area was low-lying and lacked stormwater drains, inundation during the rainy season posed serious problems. Residents also raised concerns over public safety near Krishnan Kovil and Thozhi Hostel, particularly after street lights were switched off. The association decided to take up the issue with the authorities and seek measures to improve street lighting and public safety. The poor condition of Chitlapakkam Main Road, a bus route and a State highway, and the Krishnan Kovil junction was another concern. Residents said uneven patches of concrete blocks and potholes posed a threat to motorists, particularly during peak hours. The association said it was surprised to receive a response from the Corporation Commissioner that the road would be re-laid “within three months” after the issue was raised. Residents also sought modification of the unusually high speed-breakers near a government school, saying they did not conform to Indian Roads Congress norms. They suggested reflective paint or markings to improve visibility at night. Activists also pointed to the death of a 34-year-old motorist in Chitlapakkam in 2024 in connection with an unmarked speed-breaker, and alleged that road safety norms continued to be flouted. The Southern Railway has proposed to replace the old shelters in the platforms of 10 railway stations including Pattabhiram, Pattabhiram Siding, Pattabhiram E Depot, Annanur, Veppampattu, Egattur, Putlur, Kadambathur, Senji Panambakkam, and Mosur. The shelters are being renovated as part of the project to provide minimum essential amenities such as paving of damaged platforms, improving water facility and accessway in 23 railway stations. The Chennai division of Southern Railway has already started work in Annanur and Pattabhiram railway stations after the tender was awarded to a contractor in September. Commuters have been complaining about the poor access facilities in the Pattabhiram Siding railway station, which has been completely covered by wild bushes. R. Sritharan, a resident of Annanur, said the railway station, serving thousands of office-goers, has been suffering from a leaking platform shelter and wanted the work to be completed before the onset of Northeast monsoon. body_clean: The Chennai Port Authority recently launched ‘Port Setu’ to digitise the tracking of export container movement from Container Freight Station (CFS) to Chennai Port. The system was developed by the National Association of Container Freight Stations (NACFS), Chennai Chapter, under the One Nation One Port Process initiative. This is the first phase of the Intelligent Vehicle Monitoring System (IVMS), which monitors vehicle movement using Automatic Number Plate Recognition, Optical Character Recognition, RFID readers, and software integration, including Customs’ ICEGATE. The primary advantages of ‘Port Setu’ include digitally recording the transit time of export containers and analysing their actual movements and ground realities, according to a press release. “It provides a common platform for Chennai Customs, Chennai Port Authority, and CFSs to monitor export container movement from CFS Gate-Out to Chennai Port entry and validate transit times against the Customs-prescribed timelines,” it said. It will also improve trailer turnaround time and reduce dependence on manual verification. When phase II of the IVMS is implemented, gate-entry processes at the port will become completely digital. Sachin S. Kurve, Chairperson, Chennai Port Authority, said ‘Port Setu’, implemented by NACFS (Chennai Chapter), will offer better visibility of container movement and help CFSs to optimise trailer management within Chennai Port Authority. M. Periasamy, Commissioner of Customs (Preventive), Chennai Customs, said trailer movement would be streamlined through the digitalisation and automation of procedures, helping Chennai Customs ensure compliance with prescribed procedures. body_clean: Renowned Sanskrit scholar and former principal of the Madras Sanskrit College, Mahamahopadhyaya R. Krishnamurthy Shastri passed away at his home on Sunday afternoon. He was 82. Sources said on September 23, he attended an event at Orikkai in Kancheepuram where the pontiffs of the Kanchi Sankara Mutt are observing Chaturmasyam. RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat was present on the occasion. He was born in 1944 in Mullaivaasal village, as the second son of Brahmashri Rajagopala Ghanapathigal and his wife Balamba. He studied the Vedas under the guidance of his father. Subsequently, he studied Vedanta and Sastras at the Madras Sanskrit College and successfully completed the Vedanta Shiromani and Mimamsa Shiromani examinations. He obtained an M.A. in Sanskrit from Sri Venkateswara University and then earned his Doctorate from the University of Madras, researching the subject Ishtasiddhivivarana He began his teaching career as a Sanskrit Pandit at Vaideeswara Oriental School, Mettur, where he served from 1964 to 1973. In 1973, he was appointed as a lecturer in Vedanta at Madras Sanskrit College. Thereafter, he served as vice-principal at the S.V. Vedic/educational institution at Tirumala. He then returned to Madras Sanskrit College as a professor of Advaita Vedanta. He became the principal of Madras Sanskrit College in 1999. He passed the Vedabhashya examination in first class and, through the gracious blessings of Kanchi Mahaperiyava, Sri Chandrasekharendra Saraswati Swami, he was honoured with the title “Vedabhashyaratnam”. Several Peethadhipatis and educational institutions conferred upon him titles including Shastralankara, Vedanta Visharada, Advaita Siddhanta, and Advaitavada Visharada. In 1999, the Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeetha, Tirupati, conferred upon him the prestigious title “Mahamahopadhyaya”. He was honoured in 2013 by the President of India with the President’s Award. He has authored several works, including, Siddhanta-traya-sara in Tamil, Vedanta-Prashnottara-Ratnamalika in Sanskrit, and Shastrartha-Sumanjari in Sanskrit. After retiring from his position as principal, he established an institution called Brahmavidya Bhavanam where he taught Veda, Veda-Bhashya, and Vedanta to young students. Mechanics have observed tilting vehicles, causing oil and grease to spill onto the road surface along the stormwater drain network pits. This practice has resulted in hazardous, slippery conditions, leading to incidents where individuals have slipped and fallen. Additionally, vehicles are being parked on the stormwater drain network.
