body_clean: “Decades ago, Bessy was Chennai’s cleanest beach but it is no longer the same,” says Subramaniam K.A., a resident of Besant Nagar who has been living there for 43 years. On a Sunday evening, the beachfront along Elliot’s beach is flooded with stalls facing the road, which leaves little room for passers-by to occupy the seating area. “Since the shops are facing the road, we are not able to sit on the long stretch of seating area. They tell us to move because apparently we are spoiling their business by sitting close to their shops. So, we have to occupy only the opposite seating area, which is also occupied by makeshift stalls, with food and accessory vendors swarming on weekends,” says Mr. Subramaniam. Commenting on the varieties of items sold at the stalls, he says that there are at least 20 of them selling the same thing. Some walkers also repeatedly commented that the beach becomes too dirty on weekends. Senior citizen Kanthi S., resident of Besant Nagar, says there is also dog menace. “With that, vendors and public that visit the beach also throw away wrappers and eatables. Mainly, we are not able to come to the beach for a breath of fresh air. It is fully encroached by shops and we are unable to walk in the pathway either,” adds Ms. Kanthi. Another resident of Besant Nagar who did not wanted to be named, said there should be regular eviction drives against stalls that are functioning without licenses and food safety clearances. “Some pedestrians have mentioned that there is little respite for walkers. We will look into this seriously and take action on the encroachments,” said R. Durai Raj, Ward Committee Chairman of Zone 13. Published - September 23, 2026 09:22 pm IST

summary_clean: Speakers call for greater collaboration between industries, academic institutions and start-ups; they stress need to introduce entrepreneurship as a subject at school level
body_clean: Start-ups working on sustainability solutions need to be supported from the ideation stage to help innovative ideas translate into viable technologies, panellists said at The Hindu Sustainability Summit 2026 held in Chennai on Wednesday (September 23, 2026). At a session on ‘Ideas to Impact: Start-ups accelerating the energy transition’, speakers discussed about the current status of start-ups, challenges they face and the support needed to scale their innovations. Elaborating on the importance of incubation and entrepreneurial activities, Indumathi M. Nambi, Environment and Water Resources Division, Department of Civil Engineering, IIT Madras, said not many incubators supported students at ideation stage and many students too did not register with incubators. This indicated a gap in the existing incubation eco system. There was a need to create pre-incubators that could help students develop and test their ideas. At IIT Madras, gaps had been identified after the piloting stage and corporates and industries must step in to bridge them. Highlighting that funding was not an issue for deep tech start-ups, she said a major roadblock was the trust about new ideas. Doctoral programme She also suggested introducing a doctoral programme in entrepreneurship to help students demonstrate scaled-up products and receive mentorship support for commercialisation. Speakers called for greater collaboration between industries, academic institutions and start-ups. They also stressed the need to introduce entrepreneurship as a subject at the school level to help students pursue careers aligning with their interests. Pravin Dongre, Executive Director, Indian Oil Corporation Limited spoke about IOCL’s journey in encouraging the start-up ecosystem. Various start-ups across the value chain, including those working on clean and green energy and water, had received funding with support extended for 18 to 36 months. Some had reached proof of concept stage and some of them, including projects such as eco toilets and nano fillers for oil pipelines had been commercialised, Mr. Dongre said. He stressed the need for start-ups to have clarity on long-term development. Incubation mechanisms could benefit both start-ups and industries. More support mechanisms were needed to take innovations from modular solutions to commercial scale, he said. Speakers also emphasised on the need for collaborations to address critical environmental challenges such as air pollution and water issues. Pointing out various challenges faced by start-ups, Karthika Gopi, Founder and Chief Executive Officer, Carbelim, said achieving net-zero goals did not have a one-stop solution but required an umbrella of solutions. Joseph Vijay conducted a surprise inspection at the Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) headquarters, located in Chennai, to review the various aspects of power generation, distribution, and grid management, on Wednesday (September 23, 2026). Mr. Vijay, who was accompanied by Energy Resources Minister C.T.R. Nirmal Kumar during the review, enquired about the current electricity demand and generation, the power derived from renewable and non-renewable energy sources, the gap between electricity demand and generation capacity, and the growth in electricity demand due to the prolonged summer months. Officials of TNDPCL explained to the Chief Minister the impact of the spike in electricity demand across the State, the constraints in procuring additional electricity from the power exchange to fill the demand-supply gap, the challenges in coal supply, the high cost of gas-based power generation, and the unexpected generation disruptions at the central power stations. The officials also explained the measures being undertaken across the State to meet the increasing electricity demand by strengthening the power distribution infrastructure and installing additional transformers and new power lines. They also gave a presentation on the overloaded networks, the replacement of aging transformers and equipment, and the bolstering of field operations for the speedy rectification of any power supply issues. Later, the Chief Minister inspected the State Load Despatch Centre (SLDC), which is the nerve centre for grid management, to enquire about the tasks of managing the power load in real time by monitoring electricity generation, procurement, demand, and distribution across the State. He also visited the Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) Control Centre, which functions as the nerve centre for the Chennai distribution, and interacted with the officials on the real-time monitoring of the power distribution network in the city. After completing his inspection of SLDC and SCADA, Mr. Vijay inspected ‘Minnagam,’ the round-the-clock consumer service office, established to receive electricity distribution grievances and complaints from the public throughout the State and tp ensure the fast communication of the issues to the officials concerned to get them resolved. The Chief Minister, pitching for modern technologies to be utilised for having real-time monitoring of the power situation, stressed that the State must be made self-reliant in the power sector. As part of this, he wanted the officials of TNPDCL to expedite the various power generation projects within the stipulated timelines, enhancing captive power generation, and speed up distribution infrastructure projects to help the consumers in the State get round-the-clock power supply. summary_clean: Oil majors seek to replace fresh water intake with treated water; dismissing the myth that desalination is expensive, expert calls for leveraging Chennai’s coastline; IIT-M prof says technology can help monitor groundwater situation
body_clean: It was Chennai’s acute water shortage of 1980 that proved to be a turning point for Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL)’s attitude towards used water, pivoting from dependence on Metro Water towards the principles of reduce, reuse and recycle, according to P. Kannan, CPCL’s Director (Operations). He was one of the senior corporates and experts pitching for wastewater to be treated as a valuable economic resources at The Hindu Sustainability Summit 2026 on Wednesday (September 23, 2026). The discussion on ‘Reimagining Water Management for a Circular Future’ was moderated by K. Lakshmi, Deputy Editor, The Hindu. “We have optimised our water requirements and taken several measures to reduce consumption. For reuse, the water is diverted to our processing units, and wherever possible, we have maximised our reuse capability. As part of our recycling efforts, we are also producing 480 tonnes of steam,” Mr. Kannan said. Replacing fresh water with treated water Indian Oil Corporation Limited is another oil major that is changing the way it operates. “We operate nine refineries. Geographically, there are certain things that you cannot avoid. Refineries that are located inland face challenges in reducing their water footprint. We have been recycling almost 90% to 91% of our wastewater, but we are not stopping there,” said IOCL executive director Mukesh Mohan. “We are looking at replacing fresh water used in our process units with treated water from sewage treatment plants (STPs) in the city. In big cities such as Vadodara and Guwahati, and at refineries in Mathura and Panipat, we have clear, concrete plans to partly replace our fresh water intake with STP treated water,” Mr. Mohan added. For this, he noted, the support of the municipality is required, and the STP has to be designed to treat wastewater from nearby households and industrial units. The myth about desalination Rajiv Mittal, chairman and managing director of VA TECH WABAG Limited, said that fresh water is not an answer to everything. “We have a huge coastline in Chennai. Why are we not using seawater? You don’t want to drink recycled wastewater, but why not use seawater?” he asked. “There is a myth that desalinating seawater is expensive. I believe the management of water is more important. And we should have the responsibility to conserve water,” he added. Mr. Mittal said untreated water should not be allowed to flow out. “The only way to make this possible is to treat wastewater as an economic resource. If you give wastewater the tag of an economic resource, people will treat it differently. You don’t throw your money onto the streets, so you will not throw wastewater onto the streets or into the nalas. You will collect it, treat it and generate wealth from it.” he explained. Monitoring groundwater Rajesh Nair, a professor in the Department of Ocean Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, highlighted how they are deriving geothermal energy from the sub-surface of the earth. “We are into India’s first project to derive geothermal energy from unused oil and gas wells... the ones that have been depleted,” he said. Mr. Nair added that groundwater quality needs to be assessed and different grades should be established. He stressed the need to monitor how groundwater conditions are changing over time, adding that greater attention needs to be given to conserving wetlands. “We need data integration and digital data analysis. Only when we have data can we manage things effectively. We should use Internet of Things (IoT) and AI-based solutions and integrate them under a common platform or a single body that can provide clear directions on what water should be used for what purpose, how much water needs to be recharged into the groundwater system, and so on. That way, we can manage our water resources much more effectively,” Mr. Nair said. The summit is supported by Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) as the Presenting Partner, with NLC India Limited, Larsen & Toubro (L&T), Navin’s, WABAG, Tamil Nadu Newsprint and Papers Limited, Indian Bank, Urbando and State Bank of India as Associate Partners. The summit’s sustainability-focused partnerships include Thermax as the Sustainable Cooling Partner, Treeni as the Sustainability Intelligence Partner, Chennai Port Authority as the Blue Economy Partner and Tamil Nadu Green Climate Company as the Climate Action Partner. Mangaldeep is the Fragrance Partner, Puthiya Thalaimurai the TV Partner, The Federal the Digital TV Partner and Communitree the NGO Partner. Published - September 23, 2026 11:02 pm IST

body_clean: Most accounts of the city, and I include those that were written well into the 1980s, mention with some wonder that the lands to the south of Gemini Circle comprised essentially farms with wet cultivation. But there was sound logic at one time for these. Of all such anachronisms that have survived, Government Farm Village is perhaps the oldest. It still exists in name, its address given variously as Nandanam, Saidapet, Thatandar (ouch, sorry Sir Charles Todhunter) Nagar, and the Golf Links. All of them happen to be correct. But of Government Farm, there is none. At one time, it spanned 300 acres with a fence all around it. The idea of Governor Sir William Denison, it was set up in 1865. Three years later came William Rowntrie Robertson from the Agricultural College at Cirencester and he superintended the development of the farm for almost two decades. Under him, “139 acres were under crop, and a further 36 under timber, chiefly casuarina.” The latter is significant, for the big public works of Madras city required tonnes of firewood in making bricks and moving loads. The casuarina groves we see as we drive along ECR are the remnants of the time when this wood was in massive demand. Robertson, after whom it is very likely the eponymous lane in Raja Annamalaipuram is named, suggested several changes in the way cultivation was undertaken in Madras Presidency. He also set up a School of Agriculture here with subordinate branches in the various districts. The sale of implements, seeds, and other products brought in modest revenue but the farm and the school depended on government munificence to keep them going even in the 1880s. It declared that the site itself was a mistake – “a hungry tract of land near the sea coast, ploughing the sands of which would yield little about the soils of the interior and get up no new data for the irrigation works.” The Mail also noted that Madras was not alone in this, for the same mistake had been made in Bombay, Bangalore, and other places. Cities were chosen chiefly because students for the school were easier to get. The Mail argued for the setting up of such facilities where two or more distinct geological formations existed to ensure a variety in the soil. It should be noted, however, that of all the Government Farms set up across India, the Madras Farm was the only survivor by 1898. And by then, it was operating on a very small acreage – 20 or so, the balance having been taken up for other purposes, including the Teachers Training College. In 1898, perhaps acceding to the criticism of The Mail, the government decided to add two more farms, one in Bellary and another in Koilpatti, for cultivating cotton and improving its yield. Both seem to have been short-lived. But even then, the soil of Coimbatore was studied and early in the 20th century, the farm and the school were transferred there, becoming what is today the Tamil Nadu Agricultural University. This move was also widely criticised, the college being branded a white elephant. Agriculture then, as now, seems to have been a complicated subject with no uniformity on what could be done. The land back in Madras was, however, still designated the Government Farm Village, all 300 acres of it, no matter that the Teachers Training College was occupying some of it. In the early 1920s, when the new colony of Theyagaroya (yes, that was the spelling) Nagar was planned, named at inception as the Mambalam East Town Planning Scheme, the lands of Government Farm village came in very convenient. As the remnants did in the 1950s when Nandanam was laid out. On paper, however, all of this remains Government Farm Village. Memories die out very slowly in Madras. But one peek into these tarpaulin shops and there is not a shred of doubt about their all-year relevance. And now, 'tarpaulin' seems like a generic term for a whole range of products that offer a protective cover to valuables. These shops sell those green shade nets for gardens, tents for camping, cotton canvas covers, car covers and bags (which are also covers, glorified covers). These bags are not high fashion but are made of heavy-duty material and designed to last. These shops sell these products at wholesale prices for bulk orders; and what they retail comes at prices lower than what you can expect of regular retail stores. Tarpaulins of various thickness and materials, both determining their prices, are a dominant presence, but one can always shop for more than tarpaulins. Nehru Market is next door to Anna Market, which is dominated by sale of metal items, many of them massive spare parts that go into the running of industrial machinery. The first few shops at Nehru Market are tarpaulin shops, wholesale and retail, but step inside and the shops selling spare parts for industrial machinery predominate. These two markets are not next door neighbours but closer than that, as united as two intercommunicating rooms with a common door. The tarpaulin shops and those selling used spare parts for industrial machinery exist side by side, by design. Anil Kumar of Prakash Trading Company points out that these tarpaulin covers are used to cover machinery, among other things. While out here to purchase metal parts for heavy-duty industrial machinery, someone might pick up tarpaulins too. These shops also draw adventurers who like to camp out in a temporary shelter under the skies. Similarly, those with a green thumb. The green shade nets are for them. Anil Kumar notes that almost every shop, the wholesale shops for certain, would have a tailor attached to it. The tents, shade nets and cotton canvas have to be made to order, often. Promptness is a key factor driving success and survival in this business. Many of these tarpaulin shops are carryovers from a different era, one pithily defined as “Moore Market”. Following the Moore Market fire in the 1980s, traders fanned out depending on where they were allocated a space. That is how some of the tarpaulin sellers ended up in Nehru Market, managed by Greater Chennai Corporation. Anil Kumar shoulders the weight of a legacy: the shop was established by his father Narayan Jha over 50 years ago. He worked alongside his father and brother before their deaths, and now the weight of that legacy is entirely on his shoulders. And he finds it to be excruciatingly heavy not only due to the lack of support from a kindred soul, but also market realities. “Counter sales has dwindled,” says Anil. “Demand has generally fallen with online shopping changing the way customers buy. “ So this is where it stands: much of the regular business comes from factories that use the material to cover machinery, as well as from transporters. Anil qualifies that, saying there is still demand for shade nets, tents, car covers and other items but there is huge competition from various quarters. The promise of getting items at wholesale rates or even purse-friendly retail rates continues to hold out an attraction for the cost-conscious, and they hit Nehru market. Another shop seller, who does not want to be named, points out that tarpaulins, camping tents and car covers are available at wholesale prices on a section of Walltax Road, largely Ramanan Road and near Elephant Gate Street. But Nehru Market in Sydenhams Road scores on ease of access. Particularly the shortage of assessors in Chennai, where there are nearly 40 lakh domestic consumers, has resulted in hundred of complaints regarding the low-tension (LT) consumers receiving inflated electricity bills due to delayed assessment of meters and table reading of meters (without visiting the houses). Under this proposal, the TNPDCL has also given the authority to Executive Engineers (who would be controlling 20 section offices) to call for tenders to appoint private contractors for the exercise. . A senior official said the interim measure has been proposed to ensure prompt assessment of all LT (non-commercial) connections and also to avoid complaints from consumers regarding delayed meter readings. As per the tender document, the private contractor has been stipulated to assess 250 meters per day in Greater Chennai Corporation limits, 220 in other corporations, 200 in municipal towns, 180 in town panchayats, 110 in rural areas, and 80 in hill regions. The private assessors would have to carry out the assessment by using a mobile app through an optical probe, a Bluetooth transmitter, or a manual key by engaging outside staff. While the proposal was welcomed by a section of the operation and maintenance engineers, who are facing hardships in carrying out their regular duty because of the assessors shortage, several electricity trade unions are concerned that the interim outsourcing would lead to privatisation of more works. An electricity official at a section office in South Chennai said that several retired assessors have been engaged to carry out meter assessment by fixing an amount of ₹5 per meter, but still, not many retired staff were willing to take up the job. A. Sekkizhar, secretary of the Tamil Nadu Electricity Board Employees’ Federation, requested the TNPDCL Chairman and Managing Director V. Arun Roy to cancel the appointment of private contractors for meter assessment, and said the federation has planned to hold a protest on Monday. Consumer activists are likewise concerned about the efficiency of assessment that would be carried out by private contractors, who they said, may not bear the responsibility in their job of assessing 250 meters a day. Social activist S. Kumararaja said the best way for the TNPDCL is to speed up the installation of smart meters, at least in the city, and also allow self-assessment as a temporary measure. Addressing the media, Kalaimamani Sudha, a transwoman said, “The movie is an eye opener for the public which showcases how transpersons live from childhood. Speaking about the backlash, Sudha added there’s a difference between sexual orientation and gender. “There is a need for good gender education to be imparted to the public. The general public are confusing themselves between two different sections,” she said. Shantaraman. Healthcare professionals, faculty members, medical students and members of the public took part in the walk to highlight the role of regular physical activity in preventing lifestyle-induced cardiac conditions. Prabhakar and secretary of CSI Chennai Chapter M. Nandakumaran, participated. A hands-on Basic Life Support and Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation training workshop was conducted for the public to educate bystanders on immediate, life-saving intervention during out-of-hospital sudden cardiac arrests. The event featured lectures on “Yoga and Heart” and “Nutrition and Heart”. It concluded with a public interaction programme during which doctors addressed various queries on preventive screening, early warning signs of myocardial infarction and heart healthy lifestyle modifications, the release said. body_clean: The Water Resources Department (WRD) has expedited work to clear clogged waterways in the city ahead of Northeast monsoon. However, large swathes of water hyacinth remain a challenge, and residents have called for permanent measures to prevent sewage entering the waterways to address the issue. According to the WRD, nearly 50% of the works, being carried out at a cost of ₹42 crore, has been completed so far. The annual exercise aims at clearing floating waste, debris, and large stretches of aquatic weeds in various major and minor waterways and water bodies in Chennai, its surrounding districts and Cuddalore district. Of the total 528.44 km of waterways in five districts, nearly 104.74 km of waterways lie within the Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) limits. The department has deployed about 400 machines, including floating (amphibious) excavators, to clean the waterways, including Adyar, Cooum, Kosasthalaiyar, and Araniyar rivers and Buckingham Canal. The first phase of desilting work would be completed by October first week. This would help minimise floods in rivers and backflow into micro drains by 70% to 80% during the monsoon. “The rivers would be able to handle the flows without spillover even in the event of 200 mm of rainfall in a day,” an official said. According to the department’s flood vulnerability assessment, the proportion of flood-hazard areas and population density were moving from the outer Chennai Metropolitan Area areas towards the GCC urban region. Work is also being carried out to clear sand bars at the river mouths of Adyar, Cooum, Araniyar, Muttukadu-Kovalam estuary, and Pudupattinam sea mouth. The department is carrying out controlled opening of the river mouths to prevent seawater intrusion and ensure smooth tidal flow, officials said. The monsoon preparedness works would be carried out in coordination with GCC and local bodies till the year end. Various flood mitigation works are also underway, officials said. Residents stressed the need for permanent solutions to prevent sewage pollution in waterbodies and waterways, rather than relying solely on periodic cleaning. K. Mohan, a rower and Thiruvanmiyur resident, said Adyar river has undergone some restoration efforts, including tree cover along the riverbanks and widening the river near the creek. The authorities must periodically remove the accumulated floating waste near the trash booms like in Nandanam. Regular maintenance of trash boom is essential to prevent solid waste and aquatic weeds from reaching the sea. Residents also urged the authorities to ensure culverts are cleared of water hyacinth for free flow of floodwater during the rainy season. Geetha Ganesh of AGS Colony, Velachery, said Velachery Lake and Veerangal Odai must be desilted to increase capacity. Sewage flow must be arrested to prevent vegetation and ensure groundwater recharge. Published - September 25, 2026 09:37 pm IST

The victim, Ashok, 27, from Rajasthan, runs a mobile phone shop on the third floor of a building on Athipattan Street in Chintadripet. Sethuraman then told Ashok that the money was in his car and asked him to accompany them to collect it. When they reached a car parked near Metro railway station, Ashok was allegedly forced into the vehicle. While driving towards Anna Nagar, the accused allegedly threatened Ashok, telling him he was responsible for repaying the ₹10 lakh lent to his younger brother and that he should pay the amount. When the car was stopped near V.R. Mall in Anna Nagar, Ashok allegedly pushed the accused and escaped. He subsequently lodged a complaint with the Chintadripet police. Sethuraman was produced before a court after interrogation and remanded in judicial custody. The police are continuing efforts to trace the other accused. Published - September 29, 2026 05:30 am IST

The government would implement schemes systematically he said. The Minister also released a CII-KPMG white paper, ‘Closing the Employability Gap: Role of Technology in Building the Academia-Industry Bridge in Indian Higher Education,’ at the expo. The report examines how technology can help bridge the gap between higher education and employment by strengthening industry-academia linkages, improving access to labour-market intelligence, and helping employers assess workforce capabilities. Ravichandran, chairman, CII Southern Region and president, Danfoss India; G.V. Selvam, vice-president, VIT; Nandini R., founder-trustee, GRG Educational Institutions; and Valerii Khodzhaev, Consul General of the Russian Federation in Chennai. Mr. Stalin said the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), which had promised to provide a clean government, had inducted former AIADMK Ministers facing corruption cases into the party after “washing” them in “washing machines”. “Can a government that cancelled the Parandur Airport Project be called a clean government? Those who had joined the TVK too would eventually be “left in the lurch”, he said. The ₹450-crore first close is backed by a mix of leading IIT-Madras alumni including Kris Gopalakrishnan (co-founder of Infosys and chairperson, Axilor Ventures) and prominent family offices, along with institutions, corporates and banks. “We have now achieved the first close of ₹450 crore, within three months of receiving SEBI approval. Chennai based Hathor, which is developing semi cryogenic and cryogenic rocket engines for small and medium satellite launch vehicles is one of them. Carbelim is another firm that has got funding. Carbelim’s vision is to redefine air quality in our cities through nature-based decarbonization technology. The other two firms include Quanstra, which is developing single photon detection systems and quantum instrumentation and Triolt Energy, which is developing next generation lithium and lithium energy storage solutions. The fund is looking to invest in IP-led, engineering heavy deep-tech startups, with the majority of the portfolio expected to comprise early-stage companies that have reached Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 3–4. The fund aims to build a portfolio of around 25 startups, with an average cheque size of ₹15–25 crore per startup. The fund will focus on six high-conviction areas where India has the potential to build globally competitive capabilities including Defence Technology (with focus on import substitution); Space Technology (including space qualified hardware); Semiconductors (with an emphasis on fabless design and IP ownership); Manufacturing Technology, Robotics & Automation; AI Infrastructure / GenAI (including sovereign enterprise AI) and Health Tech (including solutions aimed at expanding healthcare access). title: Madras High Court clears the decks for conduct of bypoll in Ambasamudram
title_clean: Madras High Court clears the decks for conduct of bypoll in Ambasamudram
title_normalized: madras high court clears the decks for conduct of bypoll in ambasamudram
summary_clean: Justice P.B. Balaji refuses to reject election petition filed against the victory of Esakki Subaya but strikes off petitioner’s plea to declare the runner-up, V.P. Durai of Congress, as the returned candidate
body_clean: The Madras High Court has cleared the decks for the conduct of byelections in two more constituencies in Tamil Nadu, by rejecting an election petition with respect to the Perundurai constituency and striking off a plea to declare the runner-up in the Ambasamudram constituency as the returned candidate. Justice P.B. Balaji on Thursday (October 1, 2026) refused to reject an election petition filed by a voter challenging the victory of Esakki Subaya from the Ambasamudram Legislative Assembly constituency, but struck off the relief sought by the election petitioner to declare the runner-up, V.P. Durai of the Congress party, as the winner. The judge dismissed an application filed by Mr. Subaya, who had won as an All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) candidate but resigned from his MLA post before joining the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), to reject the election petition preferred by S. Kanthimathinathan. He, however, allowed another application filed by the resigned MLA to strike off the relief sought by the election petitioner Kanthimathinathan under Section 84 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, to declare Mr. Durai, who had lost by 10,245 votes, as the returned candidate after allowing the election petition. The judge agreed with senior counsel Satish Parasaran, for Mr. Subaya, that when there were more than two candidates who had contested in an election, the runner-up could not automatically be declared as the elected candidate if the election petitions get allowed and that the only course open would be to order fresh elections. “In the present case, I am conscious of the fact that despite being the returned candidate, the first respondent (Mr. Subaya) has resigned from his MLA post and the electorate remains unrepresented as on date. But, for the prayer sought for invoking Section 84 of the R.P. Act, read with Section 101 of R.P. Act, the Election Commission would be clearly well within its right to conduct a fresh election,” Justice Balaji wrote. He also said: “The relief sought for under Section 84 of R.P. Act by the first respondent is impeding such conduct of a fresh election, which has left the constituency headless and clearly resulting in failure of the democratic process... In such view of the matter, I do not see why this Court should not exercise power under Order VI Rule 16 of Civil Procedure Code and strike off the relief sought for under Section 84 of R.P. Act.” The judge, however, said, the election petition that had challenged the victory of Mr. Subaya on the ground of having allegedly indulged in electoral corrupt practices must go for trial. Justice Balaji’s order striking off the relief sought under Section 84 of the R.P. Act assumes significance in light of the fact that Ambasamudram was one of the five constituencies where byelections had been stalled by the first Division Bench of the High Court on the ground that conduct of bypolls pending the plea under Section 84 might end up in an anomalous situation of those constituencies being represented by two individuals. The Bench comprising Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan on July 10, 2026, restrained the Election Commission of India (ECI) from notifying bypolls to Tiruchi East, Perundurai, Ambasamudram, Viralimalai, and Karur, while passing interim orders on a public interest litigation petition filed by K. Venkatachalapathy from Tirunelveli. After the grant of the interim order, the ECI filed a counter affidavit before the Division Bench stating that it, too, does not intend to conduct bypolls to those five constituencies. However, after the filing of the counter affidavit, Justice D. Bharatha Chakravarthy of the High Court on September 8, 2026, rejected the election petition filed against the victory of S. Jayakumar, who had won from the Perundurai constituency as an AIADMK candidate but resigned from his MLA post before joining the TVK. Hence, in the written submissions filed before the first Division Bench during the final hearing on the PIL petition, the ECI urged the Bench to exempt Perundurai alone from its interim stay order. The ECI told the court that byelection could be conducted for the Perundurai constituency if the Supreme Court does not grant any stay and if the Division Bench exempts that constituency alone from the five constituencies where bypolls had been stalled. During the hearing of the PIL petition on Thursday, senior counsel G. Masilamani, representing Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, brought Justice Balaji’s order to the notice of the Division Bench and said, the ECI would have to now conduct byelections to both the Perundurai and Ambasamudram constituencies. He said, even with respect to the rest of the three constituencies, the ECI “could not fold its hands and say it shall not conduct bypolls merely because the election petitioners with respect to those constituencies had sought a declaration under Section 84 of the R.P. Act.” After hearing the arguments advanced by all the counsel, the Division Bench reserved its judgment on the PIL petition filed through advocate V.R. Shanmuganthan. title: Madurantakam by-election: Will the AIADMK ‘bastion’ fall to TVK’s growing popularity?
title_clean: Madurantakam by-election: Will the AIADMK ‘bastion’ fall to TVK’s growing popularity?
title_normalized: madurantakam by election will the aiadmk bastion fall to tvk s growing popularity
summary_clean: Maragatham Kumaravel, a former AIADMK leader, now seeks re-election as the TVK’s candidate after resigning as AIADMK MLA barely three weeks after the 2026 result; while some voters are undecided, some say they may not vote for the TVK despite the CM’s popularity
body_clean: In the 2021 Assembly Elections, the ruling AIADMK was swept away by a DMK wave in the KTCC districts (Kancheepuram, Tiruvallur, Chengalpattu, and Chennai), barring one single seat – Madurantakam. Maragatham Kumaravel, a seasoned AIADMK leader and a Lok Sabha member for the party during 2014-19 period, stood tall among the ruins. She regained the seat in the 2026 elections amid a TVK wave in the region, giving rise to claims that it was an AIADMK bastion. Then came the twist. Barely three weeks after the declaration of results, Ms. Maragatham, along with five of her colleagues, resigned from the Assembly and joined the TVK. She is now recast as the TVK candidate for the Madurantakam by-election scheduled for October 6. On Friday, Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay held a four-and-a-half-hour-long roadshow in the constituency. People lined up in large numbers all along the route, which crisscrossed the constituency touching about three dozen villages. If the turnout of people translates to votes for the party, the TVK would win. But often, what is apparent isn’t real, warns Ashok, a grocery store owner in Ayyanar Nagar. “Not all those who gather at Vijay’s rallies would vote for TVK. I went there too to catch a glimpse of him but I may not vote for them,” he states. In course of a chat, he lets out a crucial fact that could well decide the fate of the election: the PMK’s position. The party had announced that it would stay neutral during the by-elections after a fallout with its alliance partner AIADMK over the choice of candidates. While there are unconfirmed reports of possible backchannel negotiations between the PMK and the TVK, Mr. Ashok says that the supporters on ground aren’t aware of what the party’s stand is as yet. “Last two elections (2021 and 2026), PMK was in alliance with AIADMK and the candidate won. So, whoever the PMK supports will have an advantage,” he asserts. Sudharsanam, representing Jayalalithaa’s niece J. Deepa and nephew J. Deepak, said, the applicant was no more and produced a news report regarding the death. The judges directed the High Court Registry to verify the correctness of the statement made by the counsel and send a notice to the applicant’s address in Mysuru to find out if anyone else was interested in substituting themselves in his place for continuing to conduct the case. The matter was adjourned to November 5, 2026 for further hearing. The applicant had approached the court in 2023 urging it to revoke an order passed by Justice N. Since Mr. Deepak and his sister were the children of Jayalalithaa’s brother J. Jayakumar (who predeceased her), the siblings would be entitled to inherit her self-acquired properties in terms of Section 15((1)(d), the Bench held. Further, Section 15(2)(a) of the Act states that any property inherited by a female Hindu from her father or mother shall devolve, in the absence of any son or daughter of the deceased (including the children of any predeceased son or daughter) not upon the other heirs in the order specified in Section 15(1) but upon the heirs of the father. Therefore, properties such as Veda Nilayam, the Poes Garden residence of Jayalalithaa in Chennai, which she had inherited by way of a Will executed by her mother Sandhya alias Vedha Jayaram in 1971, would also go to Ms. Deepa and Mr. Deepak since they were the children of Jayakumar, who was one of the legal heirs of Jayalalithaa’s father, the court had ruled. In some cases, political party names or symbols are painted on the vehicles. Commuters on Vandalur Road, T. Nagar, Nungambakkam, Anna Nagar, and Mogappiar, with whom The Hindu spoke, said that vehicle checks are infrequent and that traffic police do not monitor violations daily. “Traffic Police should take strict action against such violations. Routine checks should be conducted not only during peak hours but throughout the day and night. If someone commits a crime and escapes in a vehicle without a proper registration number, how can the Crime Branch or investigating officers trace that vehicle?” asked Sudarshan, who commutes through Vandalur regularly. A traffic police officer in T. Nagar said police regularly check vehicles and fine those found without proper registration numbers. However, when caught, motorists often offer excuses that the vehicle is new and that they will get the registration number affixed soon. Some claim that the vehicle was old and that they were taking it to fix the number plates. “Most of them are college students and young boys,” he said. Another traffic police officer pointed out that such vehicles often manage to evade checks during peak hours and late evenings when traffic is heavy. Deploying more police personnel at crucial locations could help curb the practice, he suggested. A senior official of the City Traffic police said that complaints received through social media of overspeeding, executing stunts, unauthorised parking of vehicles, and driving vehicles without number plates are fined regularly. “Already in several places, based on complaints about wrong-side driving, teams of traffic enforcement officials conducted surprise road checks at several important junctions across the city and penalised nearly two lakh violators in the first week of September,” the police officer said. summary_clean: The State government plans to build the memorial complex for 5 icons on a portion of the University Union Grounds in Chetpet belonging to the University of Madras
body_clean: The Tamil Nadu government has proposed to establish an integrated memorial complex for five icons — Queen Velu Nachiyar, Periyar E.V. Ramasamy, B.R. Ambedkar, K. Kamaraj, and Anjalai Ammal — along with a library on a portion of the University Union Grounds in Chetpet belonging to the University of Madras (UoM). The five personalities are also the “ideological leaders” of the ruling TVK. A cross-section of UoM faculty, staff, physical education teachers of affiliated colleges and sports enthusiasts has objected to the proposal. The University Union Grounds on Spur Tank Road is widely used not only by sportspersons of the university and its affiliated colleges but also different educational institutions to host their sports meets and for training. According to sources, the Chennai Collector, in a letter dated September 17, addressed to the University authorities, sought its consent for establishing the integrated memorial complex and library on a portion of the grounds. Sources said officials from the Egmore Tahsildar’s office had visited the grounds recently and had taken measurements of the plot of land. The Collector, in the letter, said Minister Rajmohan had, during the recent Budget session of the Assembly, announced the government’s proposal to set up the memorial for the leaders at an investment of ₹5 crore. Consequent to this announcement, the portion of the university grounds was identified for constructing the memorial. Incidentally, Chennai already hosts expansive memorials to Ambedkar on Greenways Road, Periyar at Vepery, and Kamaraj on Sardar Patel Road. Sources at the university informed The Hindu that a plot of land on the northeastern edge of the ground, which housed a tennis court till about three decades ago and was used for other sports activities subsequently, was the proposed spot. Over three decades ago, the parcel housed a tennis court which was damaged due to water stagnation. The court was removed and cricket nets were put up for students to practice. That, too, was damaged following which, the parcel of land was cleaned up and used for handball practice. The actual dimensions of the piece of land wasn’t immediately available. “Our apprehension is that once the complex is constructed, the pathway for access to the memorial will have to be laid through the ground, thereby encroaching upon the space used by athletes and sportspersons,” a Physical Education Director of an affiliated college said. A section of Physical Education Directors met on Tuesday to discuss the issue and voiced their disapproval of the government’s proposal. They felt the memorial could be established elsewhere on government land in Chennai, instead of taking up the space belonging to the university. The teaching staff at the university said the focus should be on developing facilities at the grounds rather than constructing memorials. Besides, they cautioned that the university should not take any decision on handing over the plot to the government without a wider discussion, not only within the Syndicate and Senate of the university, but also with other stakeholders. In the past, the historic venue has hosted the Buchi Babu Memorial Cricket Tournament, the A.L. Mudaliar Athletics meet, and even international matches featuring the women’s cricket team. Even now, the Tamil Nadu Cricket Association conducts its lower-division league matches here. “The Union Ground is common to all the affiliated colleges, who host their annual sports meets here. Moreover, zonal meets and inter-university tournaments are conducted here. Football teams of several colleges train here. Everything is free of cost,” said a PED of a leading college. “We are also hearing that around 10-15 trees will be cut and the vultures that come here regularly will lose their habitat,” he added. While stents specifically designed for animals are available in Europe and the U.S., India currently relies on stents manufactured for human use. “Fluoroscopic studies will help us measure and select the stent suitable for dogs,” Dr. Baranidharan said. Dr. Vijayakumar said government support, pet medical insurance and subsidies for procuring stents could help make the procedure more accessible to animals in need. title_clean: Why has the Tamil Nadu Private Universities (Amendment) Bill, 2026, triggered a controversy? Explained
title_normalized: why has the tamil nadu private universities amendment bill 2026 triggered a controversy explained
summary_clean: The Tamil Nadu government’s proposed amendments to regulations on private university reduce land and endowment requirements, sparking concerns over potential commercialisation and infrastructure adequacy in higher education.
body_clean: The story so far: On September 8, 2026, the final day of the Budget session of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly, Higher Education Minister P. Viswanathan introduced the Tamil Nadu Private Universities (Amendment) Bill, 2026, seeking to drastically change the statutory requirements for setting up private universities in the State. The Bill was eventually passed. The Communist Party of India (CPI), which is providing outside support to the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)-led coalition government, and the Pattali Makkal Katchi (PMK), opposed the Bill. Now, Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar has sought clarifications on the Bill’s provisions from the State government. What are the key amendments in the Bill? As per clause (a) of Section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Private Universities Act, 2019, enacted by the then Edappadi Palaniswami-led government, not less than 100 acres of contiguous land is required to establish a private university in Tamil Nadu. Also, as per sub-section (1) of Section 46 of the Act, the sponsoring body should establish a permanent endowment fund of ₹50 crore for the purpose of meeting the expenditure for the administration of a private university during the process of its dissolution. However, now citing scarcity of land in the Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) area, the government, in the amended Bill, has prescribed a minimum of 12 acres of contiguous land within its limits. For other municipal corporations and municipal councils, the minimum land requirement was revised to 18 acres, while for the rest of the State, the minimum land requirement was set at 25 acres. Additionally, the government decided to reduce the permanent endowment fund to ₹25 crore. Why has the government proposed these amendments? The Statement of Objects and Reasons section of the Bill says the State government was following recommendations of a Task Force on Compliance Reduction and Deregulation set up by the Union government to simplify rules, cut down paperwork, and make it easier to do business across States. For education, the Task Force had listed five focus areas. It recommended amendments to relevant provisions of the Act to eliminate the minimum land requirement and remove the minimum endowment fund requirement for setting up higher educational institutions. To which institutions does this amendment apply? The amendments would extend to all private universities established under the Tamil Nadu Private Universities Act, 2019, and to Shiv Nadar University and Sai University, which were established in 2018 through special legislations before the parent Act came into force. What is the rationale provided by officials of Higher Education Dept.? While the Bill says the recommendation came from the Task Force on Compliance Reduction and Deregulation, officials of the Higher Education Department say that they have examined the land-usage patterns in existing private institutions and the availability of contiguous land parcels across the State before arriving at the figures. While large parcels of contiguous land were only available away from cities and towns, 100 acres of contiguous land was difficult to find even in many rural areas. This meant that the institutions would be situated far away from urban centres, the unwanted impact of which was the difficulty in attracting good faculty. For students, too, the travel to college and back would be cumbersome and time-consuming. In the course of their review, the officials reportedly discovered that the institutions having 100 acres barely used the entire acreage towards developing facilities for students. The basic requirements of academic block, administrative block, and students’ hostels can even be housed in vertical structures, which would also make it possible to have adequate space for playgrounds. Thus was born the three-graded structure of land requirement provision. For the endowment amount, the officials said that they studied the current practices in several other States and then arrived at the figure. What are the concerns being raised? When the Bill was tabled in the Assembly, voices of dissent came from the CPI and the PMK. The CPI has since argued that such a move will lead to the commercialisation of education, which would go against the principle of social justice followed by successive governments in the State. The PMK was of the view that in addition to the commercialisation of education, the reduction in land requirement could well result in inadequate infrastructure in these universities. The Higher Education Minister defended the Bill, stating that it would attract world-class institutions to Tamil Nadu. DMK members were not present in the Assembly when the Bill was passed, as they were evicted from the House earlier in the day. The Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI(M)) members were also not present in the House. What has been the general reaction to the proposed amendment? Academics fear that the amended Bill could facilitate current self-financing colleges in the State to establish private universities or affiliate their institution with private universities. What has been the government’s response? Higher Education Department officials put to rest such concerns, stating that attempts to “convert” existing self-financing colleges that are affiliated to State universities to private universities or their affiliates “will not be allowed”, since these new entities were Greenfield Universities and not to be confused with Brownfield Universities. It should be mentioned here that last year, the then DMK government had attempted to bring in an amendment to the Tamil Nadu Private Universities Act, 2019, seeking to introduce provisions allowing the conversion of existing self-financing or government-aided institutions to Brownfield Universities. The government had to withdraw the Bill in face of stiff resistance from Opposition parties, teachers’ associations, student bodies, and the public. The current Bill treads a different line and allows for certain relaxations for setting up Greenfield Universities. What does the Shiv Nadar University experience say? The concerns are, however, not allayed just as yet. The experience with SSN College of Engineering is one reason why. The college applied for, and secured, progressive disaffiliation from Anna University in September 2025. It has stopped the intake of students through the Tamil Nadu Engineering Admissions (TNEA) counselling process from the academic year 2026-27 and are in the process of merging with Shiv Nadar University. Intake of students for the new entity will, now, be handled by the private university. Before the disaffiliation, the SSN College of Engineering was mandated to collect tuition fees fixed by the Fee Fixation Committee, as per the norms of the Tamil Nadu government. As per the website of SNU, the fees for UG degrees for the new SSN School of Engineering is six times more than what was collected from students before. This gives rise to enough discomfort among the student community. Student bodies affiliated to the Left parties have launched protests across Tamil Nadu against the Bill. They say that reducing the land requirement would accelerate privatisation of education, providing a fillip to profit-driven entities to charge higher fees. As has been experienced in the NEET coaching issue, students from well-to-do background would benefit, leaving behind poorer students and widening the socio-economic gap. The jury is still out on this. Nonetheless, this move definitely signals the government’s intentions of allowing multidisciplinary universities to thrive in the State, while it claims that it would maintain some sort of control over them. What does the parent Act entail? The Tamil Nadu Private Universities Act, 2019, entails that the executive council of the private universities include the Higher Education Secretary and the Director of Collegiate Education as ex-officio members, as per Section 26 of the Act. According to Section 50, the government has the right to call for information and records from private universities if it deems that there is a violation of the Act, statutes, or ordinances. The government also hold the power to derecognise private universities. In the past couple of decades, several standalone colleges offering multiple disciplines were elevated as “Deemed to be University” by the Union Ministry of Education on the advise of the University Grants Commission (UGC). It gave these institutions freedom to revise their curriculum, conduct examinations, award degrees, and, above all, fix their own fee structures and intake policies, removing every bit of governmental control over them. Tamil Nadu has around 30 of them functioning. There is an argument that the recent amendments to the Tamil Nadu Private Universities Act is an attempt to counter the mushrooming Deemed to be Universities in the State and to exercise an element of control over their affairs. What next? The State government now needs to convince the Governor that it has addressed every legal requirement before amending the 2019 Act. Published - September 21, 2026 12:03 pm IST

body_clean: “Madras on Stage”, the fourth edition of The Hindu’s ‘Made of Chennai’ photo archives exhibition — held at Kasturi Buildings, the newspaper’s corporate head office — concluded on September 15. We at the Library Department, which serves as the archives of The Hindu, started collecting photographs for the exhibition in the second week of July. The curator, Thirupurasundari Sevvel, suggested a division of 33% performing arts (national and international), 33% drama/stage, and 33% cinema. We chose to display pictures from the 1920s all the way to the 2010s to ensure that we did not miss out on any cultural activities or performing arts. We have in our repository nearly 2.5 to 3 million pictures across varied subjects, which include digital copies, black-and-white and colour prints, negatives, and colour transparencies. Of these physical prints, negatives, and transparencies, 60% were readily available in digital format; for the rest, we had to search through physical copies. The curator gave us helpful clues and ideas. She also shared a timeline of key programmes and cultural events in Madras over the years. Using these leads, we cross-checked news items published in The Hindu and Sport & Pastime (a magazine published by The Hindu Group from 1947 to 1968), confirmed the dates, and searched our archives for pictures. Finding some photos was tough, such as the 1927 photograph of Pammal Sambanda Mudaliar with the cast of his play by the Suguna Vilasa Sabha. Tracking down cinema stills of M.K. Thyagaraja Bhagavathar (MKT) shot in Madras was similarly exhausting. We hold only very few photographs from MKT’s films; the 1934 musical Pavalakkodi, directed by K. Subrahmanyam, provided the sole Madras-based still in our collection. On the brighter side, we came across photographs of many international performers who appeared in Madras from the 1950s to the 1990s, including Boney. M, American jazz musicians, Egyptian folk dancers, Tibetan Amdo drama troupes, Russian Ramayana casts, and Russian ballet dancers. We collected a total of 600 pictures and shortlisted 181. Out of these, 100 pictures were physically exhibited, while all 181 were displayed on a television screen at the venue. Right from the inauguration on August 14, school and college students visited the exhibition almost daily. Film and drama personalities, politicians, journalists, and public officials were among the other notable visitors. The exhibition was inaugurated by Tamil Nadu Minister for School Education, Tamil Development and Information A. Rajmohan. Tamil Nadu Minister for Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments S. Ramesh also toured the display. Historian and heritage activist V. Sriram appreciated the exhibits and helped identify several figures in the photographs — updates we have since incorporated into our archival captions. Actor Pasupathy, whose photo from his Koothu-p-Pattarai days was on display, visited with his family and spotted a familiar face in the frame — retired Justice Prabha Sridevan, his co-star in The Conduct of Life, a play by María Irene Fornes. Actress and activist Revathi also dropped by, thrilled to spot three photographs capturing her participation in various social causes. Other notable visitors included drama veterans Kathadi S. Ramamurthy, S.Ve. Shekher, and Madhu Balaji; theatre and television artist S. Varadarajan; cartoonist Madhan; singer Chinmayi; actor-journalist Chitra Lakshmanan; filmmaker Halitha Shameem; screenplay-dialogue writer Anand Kumaresan; and cinema PROs Diamond Babu and Nikhil Murukan. We’re already looking forward to celebrating Madras again next year. Published - September 25, 2026 01:22 am IST

The previous Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) government placed a strong emphasis on building the State’s GCC ecosystem, and now the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government is continuing to pursue investments in the sector through a series of MoUs.
